Polygraphiae libri VI

Polygraphiae libri VI

Johannes Trithemius

English edition by Ian Carlos Fabin

Introduction

Polygraphiae libri VI — "Six Books of Polygraphy" — is Trithemius's openly technical cryptographic manual, the first printed book on cryptography in the West. Dedicated to Emperor Maximilian I in 1508, it appeared in print in 1518, two years after his death. Its method is stated plainly rather than veiled as in the Steganographia: substitution alphabets, the "Ave Maria" tableau by which any plaintext is recast as a Latin invocation, and the long combinatory tables of the later books, culminating in the polyalphabetic tabula recta.

This is the 1600 Strasbourg edition — the third and longest-paginated of the three Polygraphiae witnesses in the corpus (1518, 1550, 1600), the same six-book text in a different print. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5; the running prose renders to the top tier (S). The dense cipher grids are only approximately captured by the source scan and are preserved as honestly as the OCR allows — for the tables themselves readers should work from a facsimile of an original edition, or from the dedicated cipher renderings on the 1518 and 1550 witnesses in this corpus. No complete English translation of the Polygraphiae exists; it circulated mainly through Gabriel de Collange's French Polygraphie (Paris, 1561), and in English only as Philip Neal's partial translation of the preface.

Editorial status

This is a machine-assisted English reading edition, not a critical edition. It may contain translation error, OCR damage, or unresolved text marked [unclear]. Verify passages used in publication against the Latin transcription and the institutional facsimile.

Polygraphiae libri VI

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapolis, formerly of Sponheim, to Maximilian I, Caesar: the Six Books of Polygraphy. To which—besides the Key and the Observations of Adolf von Glauburg, patrician of Frankfurt—there has now been added a Booklet by the same author, On the Seven Secundeans, or Intelligences moving the spheres after God: a work of most hidden knowledge, in which the principles of Steganography also lie concealed, and a method most useful and altogether admirable, as much in teaching as in learning, is shown to the ingenious. At Strasbourg, at the expense of Lazarus Zetzner, bookseller. 1600.

[Royal Library of Munich.]

The Printer to the Reader, Greeting. When, at the urging of certain persons, candid Reader, I had resolved to publish anew, at my own expense, the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, I diligently applied myself to this: that it might come forth both more correct and enlarged by a new addition. And so, having sought out various editions from everywhere, I diligently compared them with the most recent; and besides, I added also a manuscript exemplar of Jacob Trithemius, brother of Johannes, and, a collation having been made with the remaining editions, I found it nearly similar to them, a few [readings] excepted. Secondly, I appended the same author's booklet on the Secundeans, or Intelligences moving the sphere after God. It is yours, kind Reader, to take in good part this our endeavor, such as it is. Farewell.

To the Divine Maximilian Caesar: the Letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St. James at Würzburg, on the Polygraphia.

I was wavering, most unconquered Maximilian Caesar, with an uncertain mind, and for some little while I doubted within myself whether I would be doing something worthwhile or not if I dedicated the codex of my Polygraphia to Your Caesarean Majesty. For among the great you are greatest, among the more powerful most powerful, and among all wise men by far the wisest; and for that reason nothing is to be inscribed to you unless it is great, nothing dedicated unless it has been composed with the highest learning. But I, having attained no, or only little, literary learning, not without reason hesitated rather long as to whether I ought to bring trifles before so great a Majesty, since I am neither fit by talent to compose anything nor adorned with the necessary charm of expression. For I know, and cannot deny, how scanty is my equipment, how rough my talent, and that I have no vein of eloquence in speech; for which reason, also with due consideration, I held back for some time, and feared to appear before your glorious Majesty as an inept writer.

For since after God you are by right lord of the world, it is no wonder if I, unlearned and the least of monks, fear the judgment of so great a Majesty of yours, and dread to offer those compositions of mine which I know are not worthy of your hands. And when I was turning these things over in my mind, there arrived one sent by your Highness with letters, by which you summoned me to Cologne, the expenses necessary for the journey having already some time before been assigned through another. But when the letters of your Serenity had been reread, confidence soon overcame shame, and the consideration of your innate gentleness drove away fear. For I know that your disposition is most mild: since you are the most modest of all, you are accustomed to be gentle to the humble and to resist the proud. You do not know how to be vainly puffed up, nor, in the manner of tyrants, to despise the humble who are devoted to Your Highness; for just as you have no room to grow on earth, so no envy will penetrate your mind. You are the greatest, and you have also accomplished many things, and great things, no less bravely in peace and in war; by these you have attained an eternal name, and with the highest reverence you are honored, with the love and favor of all your subjects. These are the riches of princes: the love and favor of the people, and to do justice to each person according to the commandment of the love of God.

Since, therefore, all carry your name to the stars with praises and all proclaim you most gentle and most humane, there was henceforth no reason why I in particular should suspect you to be more severe, especially when in your letter you deign to entice me to be enrolled among yours. Therefore, at last encouraged by the weighing of these matters, I laid aside all fear and assumed great confidence in the gentleness innate in you. Indeed, since all draw confidence from the fountain of your piety, why should I alone be cruel [unclear]. Therefore, with that humility which befits me, and with which I ought and am able, I approach the throne of your most excellent Majesty, prostrate on the ground; devotedly I offer the said work of Polygraphia, and humbly commend my littleness to Your Serenity as a servant to his lord. Now therefore, most merciful Caesar, accept the very small little gift which I bring, in which may you deign to weigh my mind, most subject to you, not its value.

There are, moreover, in the appended system of the Polygraphia, in certain places, some mysteries wrapped in enigmas, lest the meaning of the more inward art, which lies hidden, should become manifest to the understanding of all. Just as not all things befit all persons, so not all things everywhere and always suit everyone. Therefore certain mysteries are enclosed there, which in my judgment can be more useful and more necessary to none than to princely men. For the more matters they attend to, the greater caution of secrecy must be applied in their counsels. For this book teaches princes to command secrecy over their secrets. But because Your Caesarean Majesty, occupied with many affairs, does not have time to search out the things that lie hidden, wrapped in mysteries, lest you be deprived of the fruit of my labor, I have appended a little book that extracts the kernel of the whole work, which I have entitled The Key of the Polygraphia; with it as guide you will more easily understand everything shut up here in figures. May God preserve you unharmed for our salvation. I wrote on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, in the year of Christ one thousand five hundred eight.

Table or Index of the Works of Johannes Trithemius, first Abbot of Spanheim and afterward of St. James at Würzburg.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, was born in the village of Trittenheim, in the diocese of Trier, on the banks of the river Moselle, on the first day of the month of February, at the eleventh hour and thirtieth minute after noon, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1462, in the tenth Roman indiction: his father was Johannes de Heydenberg, and his mother was called Elisabeth de Longouico. This was the very year in which the city of Mainz, in the dissension of two pontiffs, was captured, lost its liberty, and found servitude, many of the citizens being driven into exile; in the fourth current year of Pope Pius II, and the twenty-second of Emperor Frederick III.

In the year of the Lord 1482, however, in the monastery of Spanheim, in the diocese of Mainz, on the first day of February, that is, the day on which he had once been born, he laid aside the secular habit and there took up the monastic one under the rule of the blessed father Benedict, according to the observance newly introduced. In the following year, which was the eighty-third above the four-hundredth and the thousandth, after Abbot Johannes de Colenhusen had been transferred by canonical postulation to Seligenstadt, Johannes Trithemius, by the common election of the brothers, was promoted and adorned as abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Spanheim on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and presided for twenty-three years, one month, ten days, and nine. When these had passed, not without many labors, provoked by the rashness of certain rivals, he accepted the abbacy of St. James at Würzburg, which was offered to him, and of his own free will resigned Spanheim, full of useless cares.

In both places he wrote a number of little works, from which recently he set down for me in his own hand the items written below on a sheet. Since you, as a friend, ask me for their titles, I gladly yield to your wishes, so that from consideration of such great labors of his you may hold the memory of our common friend and teacher more closely. And first indeed I shall set down the titles of those works which, while he was abbot at Spanheim, [unclear] of his order, which were made in provincial chapters by order of the presiding officers: one book. On the Visitation of Monks, one book. On the Manner of Holding a Provincial Chapter, one book. On the Rule of St. Benedict, two books. Homilies and exhortatory sermons to his monks, two books, which he dedicated to his predecessor. On the Temptations of Cloistered Persons and Their Remedies, two books. To Nicholas, priest of Mernic, On the Priestly Life, one book. Against the Private Property of Monks, one book. On the Vanity and Misery of This Life, one book. A penthic work, that is, a mournful one, On the Ruin of His Order, one book. On the Illustrious Men of His Order, four books. Praises of the Order of the Carmelite Friars, two books. To Gerlacus, abbot of Deutz, Praises of Manuscript Writings, one book. To Johannes Dalburgius, bishop of Worms, On Ecclesiastical Writers, one book. On the Praises of St. Anne, Grandmother of the Lord, one book. To the questions of Rutger Sicamber, canon of Dumetis, [unclear] book. A chronicle of his own monastery of Spanheim, not a small volume, one book. A chronicle or annals of the monastery of Hirsau, two large volumes. A chronicle of the succession of the dukes of Bavaria and the counts palatine, to Philip, Count Palatine, prince elector, [unclear] book. The life of St. Hirmina, nun and first abbess in the horreum at Trier, one book. On the Misery of Cloistered Prelates, two books. Praises of St. Andrew the Apostle, [unclear] book. Praises of the Life of Abbot Benedict, [unclear] book. Praises of True Penitence, [unclear] book. Monologue of a Man Devoted to God to Himself, one book. To Ulrich, canon of Cologne, on questions concerning the Gospel of John, [unclear] book. To [unclear] on questions concerning the Psalms, one book.

J. Trithemius.

For the presidents of the annual chapter concerning the Bursfeld observance, he abridged the statutes of that same union, one book. The Spiritual Exercise of Monks, one book. An Epitome or Breviary of the same, one book. On Ecclesiastical Computation, one book. On the Illustrious Writers of Germany, addressed to Jakob Wimpfeling of [unclear], one book. Spanheim letters to various persons, four books. Orations delivered in chapters and elsewhere are twenty-four in number, making one book. For his brothers of the monastery of Spanheim he wrote forty very beautiful sermons, one book. Sermons to the people on feast days, one book. Several supplicatory prayers to God and the saints, one book. From the Greek tongue he translated into Latin Maximus the Abbot on the incarnation of the Lord; also the anathemas of St. Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, promulgated against heretics in the third synod of Ephesus, and certain letters of that same synod. He also wrote for the edification of monks a notable work, which he entitled On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, three books. He wrote also certain other smaller works, the titles of which he did not send on to me. These, dearest brother Nicholas, are the Trithemian works which, during the twenty-three years in which he was abbot, he composed at Spanheim for the honor of God, amid cares and the continual occupation of domestic business, reading or writing day and night whenever he was able to steal some leisure for himself.

Lucubrations II.

During the years in which he was in charge he brought into the library of Spanheim a very great treasury of books in every field, not only through the art of printing but also through manuscripts. For when I was with him for the space of one year, to learn Greek and Hebrew letters from him, I counted two thousand volumes in the library, of which at least eighty had been decently written with the pen on parchment and paper. I often heard from his mouth that he had spent more than two thousand florins for books, which he had not received from the substance of the monastery, which was always very meager; but since he was both known and dear to many princes, the gifts with which he was honored by them he very often spent on books. For he is the greatest lover and cultivator of books beyond all whom I know living in the flesh today. It is said by many, however, that his successor, who is now abbot in Spanheim, has alienated very many volumes.

In the year of the Lord 1504, when a fierce war had arisen between the interregnum and Philip, Count Palatine, Trithemius, fearing the enemies, withdrew with his library and the monastery’s possessions to Kreuznach, the nearest town, and I likewise returned to my own affairs. In the year 1506, in the month of October, Trithemius himself, spurred by the envy of certain persons, accepted the abbacy of St. James at Würzburg and resigned that of Spanheim. There, in quiet, he writes various works, the titles of which, when asked, he recently sent me as follows.

Of Trithemius.

To the emperor Maximilian he published a remarkable work, which he entitled Polygraphy, six books. To the same man, the key of that same Polygraphy, one book. Replies to eight questions of the same emperor, one book. To the same man, On the Seven Intelligences Moving the Spheres, one book. To Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg and prince-elector, twenty books of various questions, orations, and propositions. To the same man, On Prognostications Permitted and Not Permitted to a Christian, two books. To the same man he wrote that remarkable and laborious work of Steganography, eight books, which that rash Bouillus, not understanding it, criticized most ignorantly and most falsely. To the same prince, one book of letters. To the same man, Against Sorcerers and All Arts and Superstitions Forbidden by the Church, five books. To the same man, On the Causes and Cure of the Falling Sickness and of Sorcerers, three books. To Jakob Trithemius, his brother, an Itinerary of His Life, two books. To Burkhard von Horneck, physician, On the Peculium of Nuns, one book. He wrote a History or Annals on the Origin, Kings, and Deeds of the People of the Franks and Germans, three large volumes; he brought the narrative from the incarnation of the Lord, in the year 433, from the borders of Scythia into Germany at the mouths of the Rhine, down to the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth year of the emperor Maximilian. To Lorenz, bishop of Würzburg—

Lucubrations He wrote, for the bishop and duke of eastern Francia, an epitome or abridgment of the same volumes, three books of histories. To the same man, on the dukes and bishops of the Franks of Wurzburg, one book. On the miracles shown at the memorial of Our Lady, Saint Mary, at Dettelbach, two books. On the miracles of the same shown in the nettle-bed at [Helprunnam], six books. An Apologetic against Charles Bovillus, who slandered things he did not understand, one book. On the origin and kings of the Franks, one book. A chronicle of his monastery, over which he now presides, of Saint James at Wurzburg, one book. To Albert, of the Margraves of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, the life of the divine chief-prelate, three books. On the transfer of the same from Mainz into Saxony, one book. To John, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria, and Count in Sponheim, residing at Simmern, on the origin, kings, and dukes of the Bavarians, together with the Counts Palatine and of Sponheim, four books. On demons and profane arts, he attacks, confounds, and overturns sorcerers and superstitious [unclear]. Of Wurzburg letters, which he wrote in that abbacy, four books. He also wrote many other smaller works, suited to his own devotion and that of his friends, such as courses, a rosary, a missal office, and various prayers, likewise proses or sequences on Saint Anne, grandmother of our Savior. He wrote praises, prayers, and a rosary on Saint Mary Magdalene. A rosary on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord. A rosary on Saint Peter the Apostle. A rosary on Saint John the Evangelist. At the request of John, archbishop of Trier, a sequence on Anne, which begins, “Jesus, king of the heavens,” to the melody “Ave praeclara.” Another, to be sung on her feast, which begins: “Let them exult on this day.” A third, to the provincial of the Carmelites at Augsburg, begins, “Let us rejoice in honor.” A fourth on Saint Hildegard the virgin, which begins thus: “Praise be to you, Lord, king of eternal glory.” A fifth on Saint Rupert, duke of Bingen, which begins: “Let them exult on this day.” A sixth on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord, begins thus: “Let us sing, renowned men.” A seventh on Saint Rabanus, archbishop. An eighth on the wounds of Christ, which begins thus: “Let us adore Jesus Christ, let us mourn the crucified one.” A ninth on the compassion of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin, begins thus: “Come, let us weep with devout mind, sharing compassion with the blessed Virgin Mary,” namely to the melody “Ave praeclara.” A tenth on Saint Joachim, father of Our Lady, which begins thus: “Let us adore the Trinity, let us together praise the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit.” An eleventh on each man’s own good angel. A twelfth for the proper mass of each priest. A thirteenth on Saint Maximus, bishop of Mainz. A fourteenth on Saint Martha the virgin, Christ’s hostess. A fifteenth on Saint Mary Magdalene. A sixteenth on Saint Mary of Egypt. A seventeenth on Saint James the Greater, apostle. An eighteenth on Saint Andrew, apostle. A nineteenth on Saint Benedict, abbot. A twentieth on All Saints. And for each of the named memorials and saints he composed individual new offices of the mass, conformable to the divine scriptures. He wrote besides a little work of meditations and prayers on the Lord’s incarnation, nativity, life, Passion, and death, suited to devotion, in two books. The Mirror of Heavenly Doctrine, serving in no small measure for compunction of mind, one book, which begins thus: “The beginning of human salvation.” He also composed many very devout meditations and prayers on our Lord Jesus Christ, on his most holy mother the Virgin Mary, and on various saints, with beautiful variety; together with many great other works, which all devout posterity will see and admire. These, my dearest Nicholas, are the volumes of our abbot Trithemius, which over almost thirty-two years he has composed in continuous study, apart from those which, not yet completed, are in hand on the anvil, unknown to me. Farewell, from my house at Durach, on the fifth day of the month of October, in the year of our salvation 1515. Johannes Duraclusius.

From the letter of Johannes Duraclusius, his disciple, to Nicolaus Hamerius of Emel.

17

Preface of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St James at Würzburg, to the Polygraphia, addressed to Maximilian I, Caesar.

We read that very many wise men of the ancients, philosophers, kings, and princes once devised various and manifold methods by which they might safely entrust to their messengers, when they were sent to more distant places, the secrets of counsel, and whatever of secret mystery occurred that had to be confided, so that they might become fit for carrying them out and secure from every assault of the wicked, lest either the simplicity of the cabalists should lay bare the mystery, or the inborn curiosity of the Bacucei should bring harm to apostolic matters. Great among these, Augustus Caesar of the Romans, wishing in difficult affairs to use the service of messengers in obscurity, changed the breathings of conceived speech from clear forms into dark ones; and by the dance of metathesis, with a fine invention, he made their barbarousness, though resisting his wishes, accord at his command. And that receptive and, as it were, perpetual order is nevertheless subject to will and to the reckoning of time; although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the assault of the Bacucei, still, since it does not keep the regulated bounds of itself, it will make all who look on anxious with suspicion of the matter.

18 Preface to Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the chief mathematician, fastened round about a white bird suited to his designs, bare about the head and feet, to a staff cut back into the form of a tetragon; and when the servants had been arranged in due proportion, the work of the white bird appeared changed. When this had been duly performed, he loosed with his own hand what had been fastened; and when he had allowed it to fly away, there suddenly arose among the familiars of the inner chambers a great separation of appearances, and soon there arose a monster of a tortuous monastic image, formerly far too wandering, at the sight of which no one could think what it was. Nor did the dissension of the owls come to rest before the image of the master had skillfully bound the magpie again with a similar tetragon. Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator, using talent and art, changed the minutiae of phrase into signs, and put the diligence, or character, of his will in place of the customary phrase. In this very novelty, indeed, he used such abundance that his invention could suffice for almost all things in the world. But upon these heralds of mysteries the institution of the art bestowed a wonderful agility, so that, beyond the nature of all, with solid steps of the feet, and not by minutiae or moments, but by whole degrees, they serve the good will of the master. A king can always use their service most safely, although not without great labor and manifest suspicion on the part of the Bacucei. But Cyprian, most holy bishop and martyr of the Church of Carthage, 19 Maximilian I, Caesar. wishing to provide for the benefit of Christians, enlarged in no small measure those very lessons of the Ciceronian institution, and added what had been lacking to our customs.

Pharamund also, the forty-third after Marcomer, most powerful king of the Franks in Germany, when in the four hundred twenty-fourth year of the Lord's nativity he was forcefully entering the borders of the Gauls, in order that all things might be done safely, bound foreign minutiae to his secrets.

Chlodio Crinitus too, Pharamund's elder son, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, after he had violently subjected all Gaul to his rule, commanded that all the Gauls, as conquered men and slaves, be shorn and their beards shaved, but ordered the Franks, conquerors and lords of the Gauls, to grow their hair and beard; whence he was also called Crinitus. In imitation of his father, he wrapped the mysteries of counsel in signs both proper and foreign.

Charles, surnamed the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks after Marcomer, who was the first of the Franks to rule the Romans, with Nanno the grammarian as his teacher, wishing to adorn the German language, which was his paternal tongue, with grammarians after the manner of Latin, began an arduous work, which, however, involved in many affairs and overtaken by death, he did not complete. He bound owls with varied and many minutiae; greater than whom Brabant, or Namur in Germany, had not produced. To each prefect of the kingdom he gave single owls by art. The Northmen, having gone out from the borders of Gothia, when

Preface to Maximilian I Caesar

...when once they were cruelly devastating Gaul, they summoned bubones from Greece and prepared a safe hiding-place for their secrets, which today is known to few.

Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the deed of the Normans, described many inventions of the ancients similar to these, by which they made a dark road bright with mysteries. He first commended artrology to the memory of posterity, and invented dactylogy. There were those who, by visible accidents, discerned minute things; by their prudence night was turned into day, and without the service of bubones light shone in darkness. Concerning these things, moreover, the illustrious Count Palatine, Prince Elector, once the requester of our steganography, received from us a manifest proof of instruction.

But others, multiplying minutiae by regulated division, after the manner of barbarians overturned the patterns of nature, concealing in darkness the dances of arising shadows, and, where the secret of counsel required it, supplied the cabala to the absent through diapyromata.

Great labor is involved in these things, and [unclear] long exercise of the mind, in which no one suddenly becomes skilled for use. Necessity endures all things. There were also those whom celestial harmony taught to compose foreign words, of which there was a double use for those who understood: while one sense holds in suspense, the other lifts the mind into the ether. God can do all things. Many have tried to seek light in shadow without light, but they were quite unable, because the fire lies buried in ashes. Some practised painters of phantoms divided one wind into two at a point: one of them, a misophos, always lurks in darkness, while the other, a lover of light, a philosophos, hates darkness, loves light, and guards the secret by means of a bubo. Again, with Bede there were some witnesses whose advancing intention bound the wind, invisible to the eyes, to visible things, and compelled many plants, and no less stones and fruits, which lack voices, to speak with a human tongue. Why should I bring in brute creatures, when all things obey art? This secret is rightly preferred to all inventions thus far, through which the hidden mystery will gain strength for the small, and by no means commit pearls to swine. From nothing, nothing is brought back. The known multitude of visible things, if these are prudently adapted to them, the enlightened mind of man would know and behold wonders. But to treat more fully of these matters is not part of the present purpose; since they are greater and weightier, they require another work and another time. Matthias, the most powerful king of Hungary, a hammer harder than adamant of the cross of Christ, victorious, waged battles; with wondrous ingenuity and art he discovered many things, adorned bubones with periphrasmata, kept his own mysteries, secreted them with manifold variety, and by manifest industry destroyed the counsels of his enemies. He preferred wisdom to gold; therefore a wise, sound mind in a well-disciplined body, driven upward by desire for a higher understanding, when by the likeness of the binary it has returned from the ternary into unity, will thereafter easily rise to the denary.

Pythagoras of Samos, that philosopher, warned his disciples that the quaternary must not be forgotten, in which the first perfection of numbering is contained. For thus we count: one, two, three, four. Stop your mind: for you have ten. For the denary is the head of perfection. What are eleven, except the denary and unity? What is twenty? Twice ten. What is thirty? Three times ten. You have a hundred, and you have by no means departed from the quaternary. And what is a hundred, except ten times ten? In these things mysteries lie hidden in abundance, and they are manifest to few. For love of brevity we pass over many in silence, who, aiding nature by art, applied prudence to secrets, and what to many who did not know seemed impossible they brought by shrewd study into easy use. A cultivated mind can do great things, and he who cleaves to God becomes, by understanding, higher than the world. Many are the mysteries of kings, and their counsels are full of cares, in which confidence and faith are required; rare faith harms the believer, and often admits even doubt when it is present. Therefore it would be worth the trouble and risk for all princes to be philosophers, and endowed with singular wisdom: just, gentle, benevolent, and distinguished in munificence, so that they cannot easily be overthrown by others. Justice alone, the companion of prudence, makes a prince glorious. To the aforementioned Prince and lord Elector...

To Emperor Maximilian I.

At the urging of Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, I, Johannes Trithemius, now abbot of the monastery of St. James at Würzburg, but then of St. Martin the Bishop in Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz, began to write eight books of mysteries in the Steganography. While I was already continuing my night-work on the third book of the same work, I am going to tell the matter briefly, if I can.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1499, in the second Roman indiction, when Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite of the town of Ghent, asked by letter what new work I was bringing forth, and with what studies I was occupied, on the second day of Palms I wrote back to him through merchants, as to a friend, that I had under the hammer a new and wonderful work of Steganography, and I reported in order what was contained in each of its books. But before my letter had reached Ghent, Bostius, in the days of Easter, passed from life to Christ. The prior of that place received the letter, opened it, read it, and, astonished, as I think, by the novelty of the promises, shared it, at the request of many others, to be read and copied. Hence it happened that my letter itself, within a short time, was spread through almost all Germany and France, and was copied many times by many people; it brought even many most learned men to amazement and wonder, to such a degree that they hesitated as to what, in truth, they ought to think of me. Among these were some who steadfastly asserted that my promises in the said letter were frivolous, impossible, and false, shamelessly devised by me for the sake of empty glory.

Preface to

Others said: “Great and wonderful things this abbot Trithemius promises; if he can do them, he can do them only by the service of demons, since they seem to far exceed the bounds of nature. But if he cannot, who will doubt that he is a liar, and deservedly to be refuted by all good and learned men?” But let both be far from me, since I promised natural things.

Of all those who rashly judged what they did not know of mine, the most rash, and finally the most unjust appraiser of things to burst forth in public, was Charles Bovillus, a Picard by nation. After he had traveled through the upper parts of Alsace, he came to me at Sponheim for the sake of hospitality, intending to return to France by way of Trier. I treated him with all the courtesy I could, and, as long as he was with me, showed him all the benefits of hospitality with a cheerful face.

And since, as is usual among friends, especially those devoted to letters, I had displayed everything of mine for my most welcome guest to see, among the other things the aforementioned work of Steganography, not yet completed at that time, also presented itself. Bovillus saw it and read it cursorily, his mind occupied elsewhere; he said that he admired the invention, praised it, and took no care to understand it. Thus, since he did not ask for the key to understanding, he deserved to hear or grasp none of the things contained in that work of ours. After this, having returned to France, he repaid us evil for good and shamefully violated the covenant of Christian friendship. For when he was asked by Lord Germanus de Ganay, our common friend, later bishop of Orléans, what he had found with me and had seen in Sponheim, he wrote back falsehoods for truths, lies for benefits, condemning and rashly judging those things which he was quite unable to comprehend with his understanding.

To Emperor Maximilian I.

For since he believed that the palm of learning would be bestowed upon him through envy and falsehood, he wrote back to the aforementioned most learned man a letter full of falsity, lies, many injuries, and insults. In it, making mention of the Steganography which he had not understood, he proclaims me, falsely, mendaciously, and far too injuriously, with rash presumption, to be devoted to wicked arts, a magician and a necromancer. To his most lying injuries and blasphemies, God having mercy, I shall shortly respond in such a way that all posterity may understand both that I am innocent and that Bovillus is impious, cruel, rash, and in this matter a liar.

I steadfastly affirm, I truthfully say, and I confidently swear upon my soul, that I have never had any commerce with demons, nor with wicked and pernicious magical or necromantic arts; but that each and all the things which I have either written or promised that I would write are pure, sound, natural, and in no respect at all contrary to the Christian faith. Therefore I do not fear to submit my promises for examination before good and learned men, whenever and as often as there is need; and I in no way intend to resist their determination. That I have inserted this history of Bovillus’s rashness into this preface of mine had a reasonable cause: that all may understand that it was done by mature counsel that the work of Steganography has thus far remained buried in darkness, not because I fear the rash judgments of Bovillus:

Preface to Emperor Maximilian I.

but lest I seem to give more such men cause for suspecting similar things about me. Indeed, so far as I am concerned, I would rather appease rivals by silence than irritate them by letters, or provoke them to defamation by writings. For I judged it better to condemn to perpetual silence all things wondrously discovered, than to incur, even through men’s false estimation, the stigma of magic or of the pernicious superstition of necromancy. Let the Steganographia, therefore, lie hidden in darkness, and let it not become common to the lying Bovillan company, which is accustomed to judge matters unknown to it, and to corrupt the reputation of a good man out of the mere lust of depravity. Nevertheless, at the urging of friends, so that our rivals, together with Bovillus, may understand what a reckless and fabricated injury he has done us, while the Steganographia remains within its own bounds, we consent to bring into the light the present work, which we call the Polygraphia, divided into six books. Let those who wish read it, and let friends read this volume without ill feeling; when they have understood all its hidden mysteries, let them themselves, without envy, be judges whether they are natural or superstitious. For I know, and am certain, that all things are sincere, pure, natural, and removed from every pursuit of evil superstition.

Whenever, however, the discourse proceeds rather obscurely, this is done for the reason that a madman should not misuse for destruction the sword of defense which a man sound in spirit and mind carries for his own protection. Yet nothing evil is contained in it on that account, since perverse men misuse even good things for evil. Whoever presumes to condemn this edition of ours is himself conscious and witness that he has never truly understood it. Mysteries are concealed beneath enigmas, lest the secrets of the Bubones become in any way manifest to the Bacuceans. If it delights anyone to know these things, let the reader approach with envy far removed.

For I am a Christian; I am a priest; I am also a monk under the rule of the holy father Benedict. I love Christ, and with whatever sincerity of mind I can, I always devoutly adore him. I have no dealings with demons; I have had none; and, with God as protector, I shall have none. I have no pursuits, no occupations, no teachings in magical, necromantic, or profane arts. Whoever thinks otherwise of me [unclear], and defends the open lie of Bovillus. But now let us leave these things aside, and let us set forth in order what is contained in each book of our Polygraphia.

Table or Index of the Things Treated in the First Book.

In the first book of this Polygraphia of ours we place and distribute, according to the order of our ternary, the words of the Latin language, as many as are seen; by their use and service all princes throughout the world will find safe assistance in any secrets whatever, which, without danger to the mystery, without mark, and without suspicion of the Bacuceans, will remain forever hidden. For the Bubones, by these means the path is known to be safe, and never to be violated by any investigation of anyone. Knowledge of the hidden matter is granted to two only, if the binary is skillfully brought back to the monad. Ignorance is the mother of error, and he who scorns to learn the good he does not know loves blindness. The periphrases themselves are extended in the manner either of one admonishing or of one supplicating, and they can be varied for every visible subject of this world. For they are suited to individual mysteries, and are set before the secrets of the Greeks no less than before our own; when you have understood the things you see, do not rashly despise the hidden things you do not see. You perceive accidents; substance remains invisible. Hence the greater things lie hidden, the lesser things are open to sight. Since this has been done with reason, let no good man take it in a bad sense, since from these things every capable man could, if only he wished, advance to higher matters. For me, however, on this occasion

Index of Book I.

For the moment it did not please me to bring higher matters into the light, since an inconvenient time seems to stand in the way. I have prefixed the letters of the Latin alphabet in order to the individual words with this consideration: that the operator may have an easy method in the proposed task, and that the reciprocal party in the relation may be relieved of excessive labor. The paraphrases that are set opposite, outside the straight order of the lines, are not without a mystery of the art, since they serve the light-bearing propositions for the completion of the necessary perfection, not the obscure ones. For this reason, too, they are employed in the former and neglected in the latter. For they themselves are fixed means by which every suspicion of opposition is removed. All things have been set down according to reason, so that not even one proposition is introduced idly. For example, the farther the sun advances from the equinoctial circle, the more the days are lengthened for those who live in those regions.

Therefore, so that unity may proceed in the proper order, by means of the ternary, into the binary, the paradigm that we hand down must be observed with rather great care. And first, after he has taken prior account with intelligent consideration of his intention, let the operator observe what he is going to grant to the ternary through the binary; let him divide the day with the night by minutes, and distinguish the minute particulars of the winds, not by an alien but by the proper supposition of the phrase. In any mystical business let him diligently beware lest he overturn the established order of the art, or substitute one paraphrase for another, or grant to one what is owed to another; otherwise unity will not admit the binary, and the whole operation will be confused and useless. Let the night not be wandering through excessive length; not advancing, it will stand beyond the limits appointed to it by the art; let curiosity not change water into snow, nor let him sleep by day who keeps watch at night. Let the mind, solicitous in its ingenuity, also use art, lest the hand by its own levity commit an error which, though slight and small in the monad, is always accustomed to appear large and very great in the binary.

Only one paraphrase from any given order is admitted to the service of the secret; and, following the example of a servant, as often as the little particle of light has required it, one phrase similarly attached is taken up, not several. These things must be commended to a watchful mind, and care must be taken that the wind not be animated. After this a rule is prescribed for one approaching the practice of the art: that, as far as he can, by mystical art he imitate the single person of a man consisting of two natures, namely the soul surpassing visible things and the flesh remaining visible. For just as the soul is not seen, although it is established in a visible body, so the secret of the mind, in order that it may remain secret and nevertheless operate at will, requires the guidance of light, enduring in its workshop of darkness. Therefore, as often as the body ministers to the soul, the servant to the master, the will to reason, see that the principal virtue of the paraphrastic power in the light is preserved in its natural vigor. For by this instruction, the first of the Peripatetics will duly enter into the second, and the monad into the binary.

Likewise, consequently, we warn the one who wishes it that, as often as the leaf is moved by the wind, he should discern the property of each nature, compare the very night of [unclear] by degrees and minutes, and conform the light-darknesses. But if Phoebus should prejudice the night, or the night the sun, through which a confusion of eclipse would arise, either let unity resume the binary which it sent away in the light, or let the shadow of night be brought back to the first line of the sun. Keep fixed in memory whatever has anywhere been produced in number, weight, and measure. Therefore, when you have encountered the knot of the difficulty mentioned, count the minute particulars of the night, and also mark the paraphrases of the daylight, and so [unclear] the one from [unclear], so that the necessary proportion may follow the action. Beware lest, while the eclipse of the sun lasts, you interrupt the necessary labor.

No less attend to this: that you be mindful of the ancient fathers, Thuysco, who, the grandson of Noah, is the father of the Teutons, and Marcomer, who is read to have first led the people of the Franks from the borders of Scythia into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine. For the Franks are brothers of the Greeks and intermixed with the Germans, once making two languages from one. Hence, according to the oracle g.g., those who have lost one g. receive [unclear]. Finally, diligent investigator of Polygraphy, you are warned that, after you, eager for these discoveries, have attained the true method of operating, you should guard everything prudently and not pour it out everywhere into the knowledge of all men, especially filthy men. For this reason do not ask, since you know that there is nothing in the world so good and holy that the wicked do not rather often abuse it.

An indication of the things that are treated in the second book of the Polygraphy.

In the second book of the Polygraphy nothing new is composed beyond the first, in which only the paraphrases of the day are varied. Therefore we advise that whatever we said must be observed in that book must also be kept in this one. For the symbols of both books are arranged under the path of light into the same order, and are necessarily changed only in the meaning of the paraphrases. In both, according to the capacity of human wit, manifold progressions can be made, when the words are varied by metathesis. The [unclear] also are changed at will, if at any time the minutes are converted into whole degrees. When this has been done, a marvellous work in every respect will arise in the art, and the world, brought forth in image, will stand in the light, and there will be no fear at all of the Bacuceans in the operator. I could have put a more beautiful face upon these matters, if I had been induced to write them either by some hope of profit or by the use of my own advantage. But since none of these things induced me to write, it seemed enough to have given those who desire it the opportunity and the material to add things more polished to our inventions, and to adorn art by art.

An indication of the things that are contained in the third book of the Polygraphy.

In the third book of the Polygraphy, having by the counsel of reason overstepped the prescribed bounds of our nation, we are led to foreign things, and, though set essentially in the midst of the Franks, we wander farther abroad through the images and likenesses of barbarians. For with almost four thousand mythological paraphrases arranged in order by art, we show a very easy way to artificial unity, through which it will communicate symbolic notions to its binary securely at all times. Here the binary is harder than unity, and unless our philologist is sharpened by prudence, he will render the binary contrary to the monad. For only the ternary, which proceeds from unity and the binary, connects both in itself like a palindrome. But if the usefulness of necessary reason is extended beyond the bounds of the proposed matter, let the paraphrases be counted by minutes from the beginning of the day as often as needed, until the minutes establish the degree in which night is equal to day. The face of this image knows perpetual silence and does not fear the deceits of the Bacuceans. It is extended to whatever abundance you wish, and is varied without number.

A brief index or table of the things that are treated in the fourth book.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy we trust in the binary, which, with all obstacles removed, without the labor of difficulty, at first sight we have reduced to unity. Hence here we use a circle in great matters, a line or point in the smallest. Nor does it matter if night exceeds day, or if light does not agree with darkness, because the circle does not receive an end, and fullness does not admit a void. For they are contraries, and whenever they succeed one another, the one is destroyed by the other. A singular mystery conducive to the binary is handed down in this fourth book of the Polygraphy, since the airy wind itself, the composer, is never designated in anything other than the binary. But in that part the lightness of owls is always suspect to us in difficult matters. The construction of this matter makes paraphrases with infinite atoms.

Index or table of the things that are treated in the fifth book.

In the fifth book of the Polygraphy we have inscribed in order, on two tables, the letters of the Latins, which we Germans also use; one of these is called the straight table, while the other is named the reversed table. To these we have set beneath windy dances, so that what we seek with labor in foreign things we may see without difficulty in our own. For besides those things that have been set down by us openly, still more secrets also lie hidden within; through understanding of them a path is opened for the operator to greater things, which nevertheless are by no means proposed to all. We have also subjected letters to numbers, by which hidden things may be made manifest according to our will. Hence through the skilled operation of this book all messages are safely delivered to cabalistic persons, although the mysteries are not free from suspicion of the Bacuceans. For every form of signs in metathesis generates suspicion in the beholder, although it brings no harm to the owls. But you, who have attained understanding of this work, will easily penetrate every metathesis of letters among our people and the Latins.

36

Index or table of the things contained in the sixth book.

In the sixth book, which is the last of our Polygraphia, after introducing a mental narration, we have set out in order the minute details of almost all the preceding signs and degrees, and, with arithmetical distributions, have drawn the functions of letters into the service of cabalistic operation. One thing lies hidden here in the bark, and another is found in the common operation of signs. For just as the spirit in the blood gives life to the human body, so the vigor hidden in the art commends the operation. Therefore whoever needs knowledge of this invention should open the eyes of his understanding, so that he may comprehend what is the proper character of each operation. For we desire all things to be open to good men in such a way that, if it were possible, they would nevertheless never become manifest to the wicked. A reason compelled us to adapt the letters of the Latins to numbers, lest, if we were too obscure, the intention of our mind should be clear to no one. Yet this novelty, so that it might not be made public without reasonable cause, had to be mystically concealed under unknown signs and marks of numbering. For the winds of the night are always stronger than those of the day, and just as night intercepts day, so light shudders at darkness. What nature denies, no one ventures upon successfully. We ask the reader not to despise this laborious work of ours before he understands it, but, so that he may be a judge without rashness, prudently to remove the bark, in order to arrive at the hidden kernel. Good and natural is the work that can be turned to good use or to evil, according as the desire of each person's will is moved.

A sword is a good instrument, and is turned also to good use whenever it is carried for defense without injury to one's neighbor. But if it is unlawfully extended to the harming of anyone, through abuse a good thing is loosened into evil. Therefore, so that the good may have means by which they may prudently provide for their affairs, the Polygraphia is written by us; and so that occasion for wrongdoing may not be furnished to the wicked, the kernel is concealed in the bark under various riddles. He who is good does not abuse good for evil; rather, if he can, he turns evil into good.

What are the causes, and at the same time the uses, of this work of ours, the Polygraphia.

We undertook the labor of the present work, both rare and arduous, for no other reason than to provide for the usefulness of those in need. I say those in need, not of food, but of aid in preserving mysteries without danger. Therefore we judge that it will be worth the trouble if we briefly note the uses and advantages that can come to those who use these inventions of ours. Indeed, since in our private affairs we have no business such that we need these teachings for concealing secrets, we have certainly labored for those whose command had to be obeyed. The first use is that the complete understanding of this work gives an easy method by which you will safely, secretly, and without any suspicion on the part of any observers make known the secret of your mind, through the industry of the art, as widely as there may be need, to any distance of places, in regulated speech. What lies hidden in these things the work of Steganographia brings forth, which requires neither letters nor a messenger aware of the secrets he carries. It would be otherwise in matters admitting the light, according to the common custom of all our people. Do not take the matter otherwise than it is. The second use is that, by the service of this work, in a short space of time, you will teach a man ignorant of the Latin tongue, provided only that he knows how to read and write letters in his mother tongue, to write in Latin as you wish, elegantly or neatly, and to conceal and hide all the secret mysteries of his will, and to announce them, to one who knows the art, as widely as he pleases, safely, secretly, and without suspicion. Again I warn you beforehand not to understand us as promising otherwise than we promise. The third use is that I shall teach one unskilled in the Roman language, not only in a few hours, what we promise: to write and to read, but

The Advantage of the Work.

but also to understand, if you have prudently applied the duty of your office, that we have not thought it should be reserved without reasonable cause. For the pupil of the new art will write a language that he did not know, and will understand and interpret Latin speech composed under regulated instruction, if you command it, adequately word for word. Finally, this instruction can be extended to all the affairs and business of the world. If anyone wishes to know from me how these things can be done, let him remember first of all to show himself such that he deserves to receive it. For not all things are owed to all men, but one is to be preferred to another. The fourth advantage is that, through the extension of the likeness of the thing received, all these things can be extended into any language whatever, when the binary of the instructor has been reduced to unity. Yet not just any man can do this indiscriminately, but only he whom, God preceding him with his special grace, art and nature have made worthy. The fifth advantage is that, by imitation of likeness, we can communicate to one who knows the art of our invention any secrets whatever of our mind, as abundantly, variously, and widely as you wish, in diverse ways that cannot be known or noted by anyone else. Here is granted a manifold speech without voice, by which safely, securely, most widely, with all suspicion removed, we shall be able to indicate most fully to those who know the art all the conceptions of our mind, however difficult. And this wonderful invention has innumerable progressions, capable of all mysteries.

The Causes and Advantages of the Work.

The sixth advantage is that, through the understanding of this work, you will be able to discover any regulated metathesis or transposition of letters, and nevertheless to form them in such a way that they serve only those who know the art, and absolutely no one else in the world. And great is the power of metathesis in form and also in operation; it has several modes and is varied in many ways. The seventh advantage is that, through the understanding of this volume, very great capacity is given to those who desire to enlarge the memory without labor, whenever the seeds of minute things are set in their proper degrees. All things, for the sake of the cause of goodness, lie hidden wrapped in the secrets of words and figures; if anyone wishes to understand these more fully, let him recall to mind that unremitting labor conquers all things. For it will have been enough for me to have found the principles of the art and to have handed down a rough and deliberately unformed manner of writing symbolically. For there was neither time nor reason for our discoveries to be formed in a more polished way, lest honey produce vomiting in those who are nauseated, or truth produce hatred in those who are indignant. Every time must be valued according to its own merits, and swine are not to be adorned with pearls, nor burdened with precious jewels. All things are untimely which do not agree with the manners and times of the mortals upon whom they are pressed. Many most noble talents of men have existed in unsuitable times, and almost every day more new things are found in times not their own. What did the wondrous invention of nautical art profit the excellent versifier Bartolus under Pope Innocent VIII, which in a certain little book he offered for sale for one hundred thousand ducats, when neither the Supreme Pontiff himself nor the Genoese, to whom he proposed that his matter be bought, deigned to come to terms with him even for a small sum? For he promised that by his art he could keep a ship unharmed in the middle of the sea for thirty months, repair it when broken, and recover without danger anything thrown into the deep. But no one cared. Nor does it escape me that many, with Naso, have perished by their own genius. It is therefore better to set a limit to knowledge than fruitlessly to expose oneself to the hatred and detraction of many, for whom it is more familiar to despise any knowledge whatever than to have learned it.

End of the Preface, on the seventh day of April, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1508.

Key to the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St. James at Würzburg, formerly of Spanheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, of the observance of the Fathers of Bursfelde.

In Explanation of the Whole Work of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of [Paeapolis?]. Preface.

No one who reads these things will, I trust, judge me either proud or superfluous because I myself have commented on the Polygraphy recently composed by me, especially if he can weigh with precision what cause induced us to speak obscurely. For whatever, when made public, can do harm had reasonably to be concealed in mystical speech. But the subject that we treat in the Polygraphy, for the benefit of the commonwealth ...a method among good men is very good, useful, and honorable; and for that reason, persuaded by a rational cause, we wrote it, so that by its service we might make good men secure from the investigation of the wicked when communicating their secrets to one another. But lest an occasion be given to the depraved and perverse, who even more often abuse good inventions, for deceiving the simpler and less cautious, we set forth in it mystical or hidden [methods] of writing, and covered the truth lying hidden in the marrow with certain veils of figures. Yet we by no means doubt that any industrious man, desirous of these matters, will easily grasp everything, if he applies even a little persistence in investigating. For the things that I have transmitted are not so difficult, nor wrapped in such great mysteries, that they cannot be wholly penetrated by a studious man. For everywhere we have so tempered the enigmas of our words that they are easily accessible to learned and studious men, while nevertheless remaining inaccessible to sluggish men of darkness. But after it pleased me to offer the work of the Polygraphia itself, dedicated to the most serene and most unconquered Maximilian, Caesar of the Romans, ever august emperor of the world, I thought it would be worth the effort if, with a few brief explanations, I made it bright and open, lest the mind of the sacred Majesty, which is daily stretched by many affairs and cares, be drawn back from understanding it by the obscurity of the mysteries. For unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be the more pleasing and useful to his majesty the briefer and clearer it is. First, therefore, with the Lord granting it, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our intention, which is contained in the Prologue wrapped in various enigmas; then, through the individual books of the Polygraphia, we shall succinctly unfold, according to the order, the methods of working, the rules, and the distinctions, and the necessary matters that remain, to the best of our ability. All these things, so that they may more quickly become accessible to those wishing to know, we shall forthwith show by examples, and we shall be briefer insofar as the matter and reason permit.

Key to the Explanation of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of [unclear].

Explanation of the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphia turns upon this purpose: that we should transmit certain methods of writing secretly, by which kings and princes, nobles and commoners, priests and laymen, learned and unlearned alike, may safely, without any suspicion of a hidden secret, communicate to one another, and to any friends, even those far distant from each other, by the service of letters, whatever concept of their minds they need, as often as there is need. And lest we seem to have presumed to be either the first or the only ones to do this, we forewarn the reader that formerly many of the ancients, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by a similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and various methods and canons of writing, by which [unclear] that which they themselves attempted universally. From their number, for the sake of an example of the matter proposed, we first introduced Caesar Augustus; understand his hidden method of writing, made manifest, in this way. He changed the breathings of the conceived voice from clear signs into obscure ones, whose resistant barbarism of sound, by a certain beautiful invention, through the dance of metathesis, he made suitable to his command. That is: the great Caesar Augustus, so that he might write secretly and safely what he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by varied transposition, so that he put B for A, C [for B], and so consequently for each letter. And so that the writing might remain more secret by twisted teaching, according to his own judgment he transposed the letters and transferred them through a long [unclear] to whatever order, number, place, and distance.

Mystery. And this receptive order, as if perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time by whatever force, preserves messages sent from the assault of the [unclear], yet having regulated limits, all makes those who encounter it anxious with suspicion of a hidden matter. Explanation. Although no one can easily comprehend with the understanding a hidden secret mystery concealed under a transposition of letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious about the hiding-place of the matter enclosed within. Mystery. Archimedes, that Syracusan, easily the foremost of mathematicians, his white bird, suited to his instructions, bare through head and feet, etc. Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods of one length and thickness shaped, round or square; one he kept for himself, the other he entrusted to his absent friend. And whenever he wished to write something more secret to the other, he wound his white bird, that is, a sheet of papyrus of small breadth but of the length of the rod doubled, around the wood, and fastened it below and above with wax. Afterwards he wrote on the sheet, joined continuously along the sides into a heap, artfully, whatever he wished; then he loosened the sheet from the rod, and at once so great a distance appeared between the letters that not even one word cohered. He turned it; similarly he wrote. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this device who could have discovered the secret. But the man who had the other little rod, when he had received the sheet, attached it and restored the letters to their former order. Mystery. Marcus Tullius Cicero, [unclear]

On the Prologue.

[unclear] eloquent orator of the Romans, using ingenuity and art, changed the small elements of speech into signs, and the rest. Explanation. He wrote a book of notes for his son, which the blessed martyr Cyprian later enlarged for the use of Christians, namely in the manner of a dictionary, where according to order first the characters are designated, afterwards the words designated by the same characters are set before them. With these notes or characters we once saw the whole Latin Psalter, beautifully written, in the library of the greater church of Strasbourg, to which some ignorant judge of things had placed outside this title: Psalter in the Armenian language. But he was mistaken, since it should rather have been written thus: Latin Psalter written in Tullian characters. For each character represents one Latin word. Nor does my judgment deceive me, since I have in my possession the very dictionary of Cicero, corrected by Saint Cyprian, written complete and uncorrupted in an ancient volume, which I have seen nowhere else. And so great is the abundance of notes or characters, with the words subject to them, that they suffice entirely for writing in the Latin language whatever you wish. Mystery. Pharamundus, the forty-third from Marcomer, king of the Franks, when in the four hundred twenty-fourth year of the Lord’s Nativity he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, and the rest. Explanation. Of the Franks

Explanation

...their kings, from the time when, in the year 430 before the Nativity of Christ, they left the Scythian borders with their people and settled at the mouths of the Rhine, where Guelders now is, waged continual war with the Gauls for almost nine hundred years, and at last violently made them subject to themselves, as we wrote in the first volume of our Annals. Of these, the aforesaid King Pharamund, in order to send messengers securely, used not a few but many new alphabets, which no one [understood?] without his voluntary instruction.

Mystery. Clodius Crinitus, son of Pharamund and after him king of the Franks, who subdued all Gaul to himself after destroying the Romans whom he found in it, used his father’s inventions in secret writings.

Explanation. This king devised alphabets of his own, new ones, and gave one to each of his leaders, while he alone retained knowledge of them all in his own possession.

Mystery. Charles, surnamed the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks, who first among the Franks wore the diadem of empire, and the rest.

Explanation. This man, the elder son of King Pippin, is read to have been born duke of Brabant in the county of Namur, adjoining the people of Liege, although some assert that he was born in the village of Ingelheim, not far from Mainz. He too invented various modes of writing, and, with the grammarian Nanno providing assistance, devised different alphabets, by which he communicated secrets to the individual governors of the kingdom, each in a distinct manner.

In the Prologue.

Mystery. The Normans, who once came out from the borders of Gothia, when they were devastating Gaul in a cruel invasion, summoned owls from Greece and prepared a safe hiding-place for their secrets, and the rest.

Explanation. The Normans, wandering through Gaul, as the monk Bede in England bears witness, in order to write their secrets safely among themselves, substituted Greek numerals for Latin letters, from A, the first, as far as the twenty-fourth point, namely w or gu, according to the custom of the Gauls. This mode of writing is altogether most beautiful: in it all the letters are Greek, and according to the Pelasgian order of numbering they designate our Latin letters, as A, 1; B, 3; D, 4; E, 5; [unclear], 6; G, 7; and so consequently as far as w, which is 24. Neither a Greek nor a Latin will understand this writing unless he has first learned the method and the art of the practice.

Mystery. Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the Normans’ deed, described several ancient inventions similar to these, by which they made a way luminous in mysteries obscure. He himself [wrote on] artrology and the rest.

Explanation. This monk Bede, in his little book on the inventions of the ancients, reviewed many and various ways of writing and marking secretly, by which they safely announced their secrets to friends and spoke without voice to those present. He was the first of all to commit artrology and dactylogy to writing; by their use one person most securely discloses to another whatever secret he has, which none of those sitting by will notice, and much less understand. Bede himself taught that this same thing can be done in many other ways as well; since we have written nothing about these in the Polygraphy, we rightly decline to say more about them here. We long ago assigned the proper place for these difficult matters in the Steganography, which we do not yet think of publishing. And who could set forth all the methods of secret writing used by the ancients? For some had as familiars in the service of the art set forth above owls called Philophoti; others had Misophoti; others summoned both into practice according to the art. Again, some transposed the known letters of the common alphabet; others, under the form of barbarian letters, devised characters of their own for themselves. Again also, some used the service of visible letters, writing with minium or common encaustic; others formed invisible characters at will according to their pleasure. But the modes of visible characters for secret writing are exceedingly many and wholly innumerable, and to mention them all is neither within our will nor within our power. Among mortals today, however, three kinds of invisible characters are more commonly practiced. The first is called Dormatic, which is a certain artificial writing made on the back of messengers, visible only through washing with a certain liquid; no one can penetrate it who does not know the secret of the art. The second is called Hyphasmatic, by which writing is done on cloth with certain substances; when it has dried it can by no means be seen,

On the Prologue.

not at all, until it is seen to have been moistened in cold water. The third kind is called Aleotic, which is manifold and varied, both in form and in material, and has almost innumerable methods of writing secretly. Its writing is done on paper or without paper, with [unclear] and [unclear], with [unclear], [unclear], and various other things. Letters are likewise written and hidden in various ways and places, as under [unclear], under [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], and in other similar places almost infinite in number. But because none of these things has served our purpose on this occasion, it is therefore fitting that we proceed to the matters which we [unclear]. There is also another kind, dactyletron, not of writing, however, but of signs, by which one person can very subtly communicate to another the conception of his mind. This too is varied by so many differences that there is no one in the world who could enumerate all the species of so great a mystery. In the principal method at once, and in many others descending from it, artfully, while sitting at table, or in any other place whatever, very quietly and without anyone’s suspicion. Finally, that you may announce the secret of your mind without letters to one absent, even without the knowledge of the very person who performs the office of messenger, remains assigned to the inventions of Steganography. For indeed, since many affairs arise for kings and princes, of which they sometimes do not trust themselves to give knowledge safely enough by ordinary letters to their deputies far away, it would be worthwhile for each of them to have certain special methods of writing and reporting, by which they may be able to make their secrets known most safely to friends, especially in these times, in which, with license for sinning prevailing, nowhere in the world is fidelity found safe. The messengers of princes are seized everywhere, are plundered by savage robbers, beaten, and very often killed; nor do the impious plunderers spare even the letters of kings, sealed and closed with rings. Hence it would be necessary for your commonwealth, O most glorious Caesar Maximilian, that you put on the skin of Hercules, wield the club in your hands, and purge for yourself from these savage monsters the world entrusted to you by God. There will never be peace in the kingdom unless [unclear] are removed from its midst. He who disturbs the peace of the kingdom shows himself to be the king’s enemy. These are the robbers who beset the roads of travelers, seize the property of others; with them the earth today is full, and nowhere is the road safe for those who walk.

Brief Explanation of Those Things Which Seem More Obscure in the First Book of the Polygraphy.

Although nothing obscure is contained in the first book of the Polygraphy, nevertheless, lest its composition perhaps seem profound to simpler persons, we briefly explain those things which are thought more difficult. We have distributed the words of the Latin language in order through nine [unclear] under almost four hundred alphabets, so arranged in sequence that, if from any alphabet one only is taken after another from beginning to end, cohering with one another, they will make a fitting Latin sentence. For it will be a very suitable method of writing, most secretly, whatever we wish, since each word represents the letter placed before it at the head. Nor let it trouble you, reader, that a multitude of words in the open contains a brief sense in secret, since in this childish arrangement of ours there lies hidden a loftier method of writing more broadly and much more secretly whatever you wish, which public reason has forbidden us to make plain to all. But he who is endowed with talent, and applies the powers necessary for inquiry, will find subtler things among the doctrines hidden in these matters, and will clearly understand more wondrous things, marvelously unknown before. Nevertheless, this open method of writing

Exposition.

the method will suffice for everything, since you can repeat it as many times as you wish, and the repeated narrative will always be varied. For if, as we have said, you take one word from the first alphabet, likewise one from the second, and so consequently one from each, and one from those inserted outside the ordered line, as far as the period or the end of the book, a Latin and sufficiently coherent discourse will arise for you. Care must be taken, however, that at one time, all at once and at once, more than one word not be taken from one alphabet, and that the writer, through negligence or excessive haste, not skip over some alphabet and confuse the narrative. By “day” understand the open narrative, but by “night” the hidden and secret one, which should not be too long but brief. The examples that follow in the text, concerning the invisible soul and the body that is seen, pertain to both narratives, the hidden and the manifest. Whenever “the leaf is moved by the wind” and the rest occur, we advise that you so number the secret narrative against the open one that both may end together at the close of any given period. But if anything remains over from the secret matter, let it be enlarged with such moderation that both narratives end at one point, lest a confusion of eclipse be produced. The other things that follow in the first instruction of the explanation of the Polygraphia are also implicitly referred to all the things we have said. But it must be noted that under the order of the alphabets there is no idle word; rather, each one represents the letter placed before it at the head. Since the reader may lack perfect knowledge of this matter, let us explain the meaning by an example.

Of Book I.

Let us suppose the case that a wicked man seeks through you to be advanced with some friend of yours; but you, in order to cut off his importunate requests and yet not advance an unworthy man, decide to write more secretly to your friend by means of the very man who is asking, so that he may not understand: “Beware of that man, for he is a thief and a very bad scoundrel.” Go to the first alphabet; write the word Conditor, which signifies C; in the second, clemens, which gives A; in the third, decernens, which represents V; in the fourth, mundana, which signifies E. Now you have in the hidden narrative: caue. Consequently, also through the other alphabets, [unclear] signifies: “the seraphic pleasantness with all his saints in heaven, amen. The gentleness of the most glorious prince, to be remembered everywhere reverently by the saints, by the best precepts exhorts us, most abject sleepers, because of the reverence of the director of good men, to leave the present things behind, and with every affection, according to our powers, to await the glory of perpetual rest. Therefore receive instruction, O vain mockers, so that you may be able to enter, most happily adorned, into the most blessed dances of the archangels of the rewarder of the orthodox. Rise, therefore, from the most filthy honors of this pilgrimage, since you are about to enter, most holily, into the joys of the kindly savior of the ages, most blessed.” In this public narrative written above there is contained this sentence, hidden in secret, namely: “Beware of that man, for he is a thief, a very bad scoundrel; but keep silent, I beg you.”

Exposition of Book I.

The same order must be followed in all other cases whatsoever, beginning from the head as many times as necessary until you have manifestly enclosed the hidden narrative of your secret. But the words that are placed outside the alphabetical order designate no letter and do not serve the hidden narrative, but have been inserted because of a lack of synonyms, so that the sequence of Latin speech might be completed. For we could not always have so many signifying words, especially among pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections, that we could have made an alphabet in place of the twenty-four wandering letters, as is clearly evident after the eighth alphabet, where we placed two words outside the order, lest we leave the discourse defective. For thus we placed: “with all,” and thus: “with all together.” The writer may take whichever two of these he wishes, whenever he finds similar ones. Let him do likewise in other cases, which we often need in our German language. For one who is ignorant of Latin speech may write his hidden secret in German beneath a Latin discourse without any difficulty.

Se-

57

Now follow the rules or cautions to be observed in the operation of this book.

The first rule or caution advises you that the secret of your mind, which you wish to announce to an absent friend who knows the art and has the book of the Polygraphia, you should write as carefully as you can on a sheet, in the Latin language or the German, or in any other you wish that can be represented by Roman letters. Then place the sheet so written before you, so that for each individual letter of the secret you may be able to fit an appropriate word. For, as we have shown, in this practice of writing a whole word is taken. We gave an example a little earlier in the foregoing.

II. The second caution instructs you that, as has been said, you should not take more than one word at the same time from an alphabet in one narrative of the public Latin discourse; otherwise you would both confuse the open sense and entirely draw away from understanding the mystery the friend to whom you had written.

III. Third, one must take the greatest care not to skip any alphabet through negligence, without taking from it one word fitting the secret.
