To him be praise, honor, virtue, and glory: he who, through the innocence of his death, freed our race from the destruction of eternal perdition, and, with perpetual mercy, opened again the entrance to eternal life for all who believe in him with a pure conscience. Line by line we have set down three hundred and eight paraphrases, deliberately avoiding a longer wandering [unclear]. For it seemed enough to us at the beginning of this lucubration if we gave those wishing for larger matters a reason to seek them out, since both time and method for these things were lacking to us. Farewell, friendly reader. From Peapolis, on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508. IOAN-

460

The third book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

What, from the beginning of human creation, confused the unity of language? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing outward those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself. Yet of this ministry of the mind’s secrets to the senses there are many modes, whose properties vary both by use and by art. Use, introduced at pleasure, is common to many; art, however, to few. Indeed no one will readily estimate how much the very unregulated use of speaking among the Germans alone has varied in six hundred years, who has not rather often reread Otfrid, monk of Weissenburg, in the poems of the German tongue. The sea flows and ebbs; men, once dying, do not return again to the present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines with respect to better things.

Who today among the Germans, ancient emulators of the Greeks, possesses the old knowledge of idioms? In the chronicles, the ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibaldus, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed many things said in old verse, in the prose of the German speech, into their compositions, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, Thuringians, daily undergoes notable variation? Men are changed in time, customs vary, minds are changed, clothes vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient property of idioms is varied; nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a vicissitude of all things; variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to reduce this perpetual flowing away, so to speak, to the concord of unity?

But the fact that we add a third to the preceding books of the Polygraphy has not lacked a special reason. For, since the wills of men are various, rightly there are given manifold modes for honorable operations. In those, day illuminates night; in these, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, the blind illuminates the blind, and, existing and remaining sight without eyes, ministers in darkness what it does not have. Here night darkens day with perpetual gloom, and one walking in darkness without light provides blind guidance. These paraphrasms serve all men throughout the world, and in every language transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latinity moves barbarians to laughter, and barbarism itself produces suspicion among Latin-speakers. Yet it matters nothing or little, since however great suspicion may have been, it will nevertheless contain every most secret mystery. Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts which we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed; without it the usefulness of no art will stand. Thus in a few things we have shown the way to the greatest matters, and, with a finite mode, we have given the way to infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared for friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be fixed in every place until you take up the mark of rest. Farewell. From Peapoli, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

We have entrusted the night, safely serving hidden things, to be guided by the shadows of periphrases; we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines all the way to the end, adapted for the use of those who wish to employ them. The places of minutes, having fixed degrees, are three thousand one hundred and fifty, although, if you wish, infinite moments of hours remain for concealing, in every language of every nation of the world, whatever secret matter may arise. The circle, arising linearly from a point, as far as you wish and as the work requires, you will be able to lead back to the path by which you came. If much of the night remains, lead back the dragon's tail to the original tail-place at the head. But the binary is made altogether certain from the known signs of unity. Let him who rages greatly labor greatly, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is there need of great labor to lead wherever you wish that which proceeds of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set an end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell.

From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh indiction.

508 The Fourth Book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James the Greater, apostle, at Wuerzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The order of reasoning demanded that our fourth book of the Polygraphia be made unlike the preceding ones in quality, invention, and facility, so that those wishing to share in secret matters may attain this not by one method but by various and different ones. We have extended a system easily comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that the night, always connected through the minute to the monad in whatever order, may be recognized in the light of day. Here there is found no disagreement between unity and the binary; nor will it be necessary for the person wishing to operate the instrument of the art to have it at hand, when pri-

[unclear], succeeding the first with the middle as end, reveals the hidden mystery. Hence the prudent man, understanding and experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. Knowledge of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun with even a single point. Although it can also happen that the knower becomes skilled without the guidance of a teacher. Yet I think this is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning those that follow, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic modes of secrets that we have presented, the progression of this fourth book, easier than the rest, can be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the cause of the example. The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. Written at Peapoli, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

With the possibility of our new invention demonstrated, which has been shown briefly and no less sufficiently, I do not think that on this occasion I myself should be wearied any longer in the same matter, since the method offers a path to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding books, since a discerning reader, if he is studious, can, with the Lord’s help, discover even the greater things that lie hidden in these. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the reason; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass our work by his own talent. But whoever desires this [unclear] to be more beautiful in the shade, let him join hand and mind to talent, and let him make a path for himself, more beautifully adorned with paraphrase. Let anyone whom these things delight keep fixed in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men, and finally there are almost infinite terms for things, villages, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that a book and a method can be made, not impossible, if talent is at hand with diligence, which may surpass our inventions without limit. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the more subtle matters that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we join the fifth.

The fifth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, begins.

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have arranged as best we could in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphy, reasonably require that in the fifth book we briefly discuss the remaining precepts of this instruction, the methods that still remain. Therefore in it we shall give a sufficiently compendious method by metathesis, that is, the transposition of letters, by which a friend may securely, safely, and most secretly write to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used that method of writing in secret matters. Although this method of sending messages is in many ways secure, nevertheless to observers it is always regarded with suspicion, because as soon as the transposition of letters is seen, anyone who is curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from these, for a necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, reserving the rest to be investigated by his talent. First, therefore, we have placed at the head a canonical table of this practice, beneath which we have set another, reversed. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforementioned transposition is entirely placed, upon which the structure of the whole building is set. For when these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to escape one who works diligently. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might give the reader abundant means of transposing letters. The use of these consists, according to one’s wish, in each individually, or, if you prefer, also in all together. If you have secret correspondence with many people, distribute the individual alphabets to your individual acquaintances, but commit to memory what you have handed to each one. To the first, indeed, let the first alphabet be entrusted, to the second the second, to the third the third, and so let it be done in sequence with the rest. But if, because of a multitude of business or of household members, the alphabets which we have marked should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and evident, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, the number of which may always remain perpetually hidden. Let us set down an example of this matter: let b be a, let f be b, let p be c, let t be d, let z be f, let c be g, let m be h; so consequently through the whole usual alphabet let it be arranged that between any letter assumed and its substitute three idle and transposed letters lie between. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, in such a way, however, that the whole alphabet, as if revolved into a circle, meets together, but each letter is placed for another in its own order in the same series. In whatever way you write it, you must know that it is to be firmly entrusted to memory, lest through forgetfulness

554. Polygraphy, Book V.

…[such] a lapse that you yourself can no longer read what you had written. For the transposition of letters is possible in as many ways as—according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in a mortal body by temporal operation, does not properly grasp the infinite—a mortal but innumerable number rises up. Whence whoever shall wish to have more modes of writing by metathesis, and ones remote from our system, if he be but a little ingenious and diligent, will easily achieve the effect in his own working. For the talent of man can [accomplish] the greatest things, if it be aided by study and art. But he who spurns the least things will never attain to the greater. I know there will be very many who will deride these our studies as vain and childish; to whom we give for answer that we shall be entirely content, provided they please those for whom they were composed.

There follows the Straight Table.

555. The Straight Table of Transposition.

[transposition grid, as printed] In this canonical or straight table of letters you have, from our one and usual [alphabet] of Latin letters themselves, by their permutation or transposition, as many alphabets as there are monograms throughout it—namely four-and-twenty times twenty-four, which make in number 576; and multiplied by as many again, they yield a little less than fourteen thousand.

556. The Reverse Table of Transposition.

[reverse transposition grid, as printed] In this reverse table you have, by the transposition of letters, as many alphabets as we marked in the preceding straight [table]. For, as you see, under the metathesis there are 24 to the right; to the left likewise as many; downward 23; and upward 23. Which, multiplied 24 times by 93, reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, make alphabets not fewer than 112.

There follows the same table expanded.

[expansion grid, as printed] This is the first figure of the expansion of the straight table, having five alphabets by metathesis, with the letters transposed as is seen. For in the first alphabet, for a is taken b, for b is taken e, and so on consequently, as appears more clearly to one looking. In the second alphabet, for a let c be taken. In the third, d; in the fourth, e—as the placement of the order teaches.

Let the expansion be continued.

Johannes Trithemius [Peapolitanus?] to the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the painstaking Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve for the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews established twenty-eight signs of certain duplicated letters, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, with like foresight remedied this deficiency of letters by the addition of four characters. We, therefore, having twenty-four letters, why do we not make ours numerical too, since we can likewise find four duplicated ones? Let us give four as an example, and that will be sufficient for every number: m and final iij; likewise r and final 2; likewise long s and final, or closed, s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-four letters in common use, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers.

And it will be no very laborious matter to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they once commit it to memory. For this invention of ours will be able to comprise many thousands upon thousands in number, all of which can be distinguished and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. Many, less experienced in the art of reckoning, think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of the algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have inspected with your eye a number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is so easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number.

I wrote this on 16 March, in the year 1508.

O JOAN-

578

Here begins the sixth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg.

Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still rude in intellect and uncultivated in morals, under the rule, shared by alternation, of three intelligences, as certain persons think, succeeding one another in order through one thousand sixty-three years, the influences of the planets in the sphere are said to have presided in their own way over bodies on earth by their influence, chiefly under the governance of their intelligence, whom they called Orisiel, that is, the life-giver of God, for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and as many days and hours. These things we recount as poetic, not as affirming them.

After Saturn, Venus is set down as having assumed dominion; after Venus, Jupiter. But after Jupiter, Mercury, the fourth ruler in order, adorned human talents with various arts. Under the three intelligences already mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence, whenever one person wished to announce something secret to another, he did it not by writings, since the function of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees, plants, or of some other sensible things, just as they had agreed among themselves.

The time of Saturn, as they say, gave to human beings morals properly suited to his influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, woodland-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and morals, living for a long time in the flesh. After Orisiel of Saturn, as those who hold this opinion say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, receiving the government of the world by influence, continued it for three hundred fifty-four years, and for four months, days, and hours; under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities more frequently, and also to discover various manual arts, namely weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to flow away much more into pleasures of the flesh, and to take beautiful wives, and, many children having been begotten by them from these wives, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and more eagerly devised whatever they affirm to pertain to the influence of Venus, following the motion of the flesh.

They named the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel; when it received dominion of the world after Anael, it made human beings restless with desire for ruling, to carry on hunts, to make tents, and to adorn themselves with various garments. While he was ruling, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, a great division arose between the good and the bad: the former calling upon God, but the latter given over to the flesh and to the world. Under his rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

But the fourth mover or angel of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year of the world at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. But the letters then, as they report, were very different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time afterward these were changed in many ways, and took on an easier manner of formation and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding deity of all literature, promising that great secrets of things lay hidden beneath fables. After this, when the human race had multiplied and had been spread everywhere over all the earth, the unity of letters did not remain long; rather, the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered different and various modes of writing, about which our narration is long. Plato the Philosopher

[unclear] in the Phaedrus relates that letters and the use of writing, together with the system of weights and the game of dice, were first invented by a certain philosopher named Theuth, and that he taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost every nation and people, letters that remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose to set down or describe the account. For all the more learned men among us know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α, ε, γ, δ, ζ, ω, λ, μ, ν, ι, θ, ξ, π, σ, τ, ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: ξ, θ, φ, χ. And Pythagoras afterward added the letter u, so that there would be twenty in all; ζ, κ, ω were subsequently invented by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters of their own. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters too was varied in many ways. Hence it came about that the use of letters in the course of time arrogated to itself such license that not only individual peoples, but also particular men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding-places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unfamiliar character will not be free from suspicion among those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a private mode of writing, separate from the common one, caring little for the suspicion of others, provided that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. Moved by imitation of these, and desiring to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as possible, to a finished end, in this sixth book, which is also the last, I have resolved to recall from the dead certain characters of the ancients, which long ago passed out of human use, lest they perish entirely; and first indeed we shall set down the ancient mode of writing of the Nortmanni.

On the Alphabet and Wonderful Mode of Writing of the Nortmanni, at the Time When They Were Ravaging [unclear].

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said before, whereas of the Latin letters, which we Germans also use, only seven are counted as numerals, namely c, d, i, l, m, y, and x. The Nortmanni, however, together with the Asiatic Dacians, having gone out from the Scandian islands, which are now called Gothic, overran Gaul for more than forty years and laid it waste most grievously. In order to provide for their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk bears witness, they devised a new and elegant mode of writing from the letters of the Greeks, as follows. For they adapted the numerical values of the Greeks, comprised in ten of their twenty-four letters, to Latin characters, and under a foreign appearance prudently concealed our letters, in precisely the way in which we use numbers in place of letters, that is, when for a we put 1, for b 2, for c 3, for d 4, and so on in succession to the end of the alphabet. It is indeed a fine and quite secure invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six; and in this mode of writing, representing f, the sixth letter of the Latins, and, in addition, deferring to our German language in which we were born, we have put double w as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation at the end, which, according to the Greek number, we have formed thus: [unclear]. We shall set down this script of the Nortmanni from the following order of Greek letters by imitation.

[Figure: O 4 Hiins.]

By the service of this alphabet the Normans wrote, in a secure communication, whatever they wished to keep hidden among themselves. No Greek could understand this method of writing, since, although all these characters are Greek, nevertheless they represent Latin letters according to numerical order; nor could it be understood by a Latin who had not first acquired knowledge of this art. This mode of writing can also be varied in many ways, when by transposition the numbers and the letters are changed. This can also be done with the usual Greek letters, at the wish and discretion of any industrious writer. Nor will the manner of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has been somewhat accustomed to it. The characters written above are also sufficiently suited to the German language; with them we can denote everything that occurs to us, in whatever speech we may be skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter k, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above.

On the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks

The opinion of many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they also steadfastly affirm that they used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. For they say that great consonance exists between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned former teacher of mine, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, the most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in the Commentaries that the ancient Druids in Gaul, the priests of sacred rites, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But as the Romans devastated the world, they at last violently imposed, together with their dominion, the use of their letters upon many nations.

Finally, the remnants of the Trojans, who afterward were called Franks, in the four hundred and fortieth year before the incarnation of the Lord, having gone out from the territories of the Scythians, with King Marcomer providing leadership, came into Germany and received settlements at the mouths of the Rhine from their brothers the Saxons. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years they waged an almost continuous war with the Romans and the Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, and at last subjected almost all Europe to their empire or kingdom. Yet they did not abolish the letters of the Romans once they had accepted them; rather, mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they themselves learned their language, and preserved their letters and form of writing.

The writer of the histories of this people, Wastbald, wrote in his native tongue books of the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes through almost seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the characters appended, as Hunibald says, which he mentions in his volume that he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

From the Grammatical Writings of Otfrid, Monk of Weissenburg

We read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, attempted, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, to regulate the German language. And when, as Turpin bears witness, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being delayed by frequent incursions of wars, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; nor did another arise after him who would bring the care of this matter back to mind.

But the aforesaid Otfrid, a monk, formerly a hearer and disciple of Rabanus of Fulda, under Louis the Pious, son of that Charles, having acquired that grammar, though imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound forth the admirable weight of regular instruction. For he composed many poems according to that same standard, in heroic meter and also in elegiac, and in addition composed some works in prose, addressed to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also to Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others.

Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too extracted these present characters of the alphabet from many, lest they utterly perish. It is established, moreover, on Otfrid’s testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, which he might use securely, throughout his very broad kingdom, in secret matters with individual prefects. From these, with Otfrid supplying them, we entrust a few things to these letters.

ZI A P Z T N 7 t † B L H C O G V X K S m I U R Q Y T D F K L ß T ψ z C o e Λ m ψ s Ψ w Charles the Great, most Christian king and emperor, waged war with the Saxons for no fewer than thirty years, whom at last, overcoming them by the sword, he converted to the Christian faith. But fearing that they would again apostatize from the faith, as they had done several times, he appointed certain secret investigators, to whom he granted judicial power, so that, traveling through all Saxony, they should secretly and diligently inquire concerning the faith and morals of the people; and whoever they found to have apostatized from the faith, robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, despisers of the Church and of its priests and commandments, or those disturbing the Christian commonwealth with notorious crimes, or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they should without delay, by imperial and royal authority, hang with a noose with impunity, or otherwise kill as they could.

And so that this institution might remain forever unshaken, he gave the same men power also to appoint others, suitable under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid faculty, should exercise with impunity the office of inquiry and of death against the guilty. Finally, he prescribed for them secret laws and hidden signs, together with a form of oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, being mutually known to one another, might remain hidden from others, and preserve forever the necessary, more secret judgment in Saxon land. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, all of which at length entirely fell out of use. Nevertheless the office of this sort of inquisition remains down to the present time; its ministers are commonly called Feimeri.

Although these characters do not appear sufficiently beautiful and elegant, nevertheless it pleased me to join them with the aforesaid new inventions of mine, because of honor and reverence for antiquity, since there is no one even a little diligent who could not devise more beautiful ones for himself according to his own judgment. Yet continued practice in writing will be able, with easy compensation, to correct this misshapen crookedness, and, when frequently brought into habit, to make it pleasing. For no one, however learned or skilled in any language, also becomes a good writer unless by long practice he has transformed use into art. Another follows.

The first is that he form characters easy to handle; and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he arrange the individual letters in such a way that, when joined into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. I add a third, not promised: if you want the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, in the manner of the Hebrews.

[unclear] This Frank came with Marcomer from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the Rhine in Germany, and, as a supplement to the German language, is said to have invented these characters, which also seem to agree with it sufficiently in many respects. Pharamund too, king of the Franks in Germany after Marcomer, who had brought the people in, the forty-third, and he died in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 426, when he had sent his scouts through Gaul for the purpose of invasion, ordered them to write in such characters.

Besides that alphabet of the Northmen which we placed at the beginning of this sixth book, we have also found the following written out in Bede.

From Latin letters also multiple alphabets are made, when, either reduced to number according to the model which we handed down in the preceding fifth book, or otherwise, in imitation of the Northmen, together with Greek letters they provide a method even for our own letters, for communicating most securely whatever we wish. Let us consequently set down, according to the number and order of our usual alphabet, the letters themselves changed in an unusual way, and we shall have a secret and mystical method of writing, sufficiently fine and elegant, confirmed by usage. This method of numbering, however, is different from the one which we placed in the fifth book, and is more suited to our purpose.

Vanity, fraud, craftiness, deception, sophistry, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the handmaids of alchemy; pretending that their mistress is beloved, they keep her inviolate, and readily prostitute themselves to those moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers after her.

On the Notes and the Wondrous, but Excessively Laborious, Method of Writing of M. T. Cicero, and after him of St. Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of notes of no small size. St. Cyprian, bishop of the Carthaginians and martyr, enlarged it with many notes for words, adding terms necessary for the uses of Christians, so that the work itself became useful not only to pagans, but much more also to the faithful. The codex is rare; I have found it only once, and bought it for a low price. For when, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1496, I was examining several libraries out of love of books, I found the aforementioned codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected because of its great age, thrown under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, at how much he valued it. He answered that he would prefer to it the little works of St. Anselm recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter occurred in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested little works of Anselm for the sixth part of a florin, handed them over to the rejoicing abbot and monks, and rescued the codex, which was already close to perishing. For they had decided, out of love of the parchment, that it should be scraped. Almost two years after this, I went up on horseback to Strasbourg on affairs of my order and, being admitted by Johannes Keisersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the major church, I found an entire Psalter written out in the same notes of Tullius and Cyprian, and most elegantly written with golden chapter initials. But the title had been placed on the outside by someone ignorant of the mystery as follows: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I brought in a scholar, showed the falsity, and advised that it be rewritten thus: “Psalter written in Ciceronian notes.” Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, since I did not afterwards return to that library. So that you may see, reader, the form of Cicero's notation, we have determined to set down a few notes below.

How we can safely write any secrets whatever, both with numbers and in many other varied ways.

These things are childish, I admit, since anyone, according to his own capacity and judgment, can devise many alphabets more elegant than those we have recorded in this volume. For that reason we knowingly omit many things which, by the same reasoning, we judge to be childish, common, and of little use. I fear that someday I shall be ashamed to have directed my mind to these trifles, while more useful matters were left aside. But let the readers spare me, I pray: my own will indeed drew me back from these childish studies, not to say at least in part vain ones, but the insistence of certain friends compelled me to write them; to them I neither could nor should deny this without injury to the bond contracted between us. Nevertheless, induced by their entreaty, I also had to connect the following chapter with what was prescribed above: to set numbers in place of letters. For the ancients established various and manifold methods of writing by means of numerical figures, by which, through subtle invention, they safely transmitted their secrets to one another. And so, persuaded by the prayers of my friends, we have placed, at the end of this sixth book, a few methods out of many, by which a path may lie open for the ignorant toward knowledge of the others. For if anyone takes pleasure in knowing these things, he will easily be able, from those once known, to climb to higher things, and to vary the methods discovered by manifold interchange according to his own judgment. As a beginning for this matter we have placed a table under the orchema, which, when the reading is varied in the manner of a caterpillar, will contain in itself ninety-six alphabets.

To the seven Planets we have assigned alphabets singly, from the numbers remaining after the twelve signs. And note: when in speech a letter is doubled, its number is not written twice, but once, and marked above with a point.

The Sixth and last book of our Polygraphy we have, by God's mercy, brought to its conclusion; in which, concluding our discourse with the wandering stars, we forewarn the reader on certain points. First, that as often as he uses the alphabet of any sign or planet, he should prudently add the character of the same, for the sake of a twofold usefulness. For by this the excessive labor is removed from the friendly Reader, [and] the mystery will remain in secret, while anyone ignorant of the art will suppose the table written in numbers to pertain to signs or planets, [and will] not suspect that any mystery at all lies hidden. [...the source here is corrupt...] For the shrewd Reader, who is touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he detects the function of a single number, will easily reckon out the whole alphabet. Secondly, remember—whoever you are that desire to be a shrewd operator in this matter—that [a doubled letter] is written but once and marked above with a point. As, for example: I wish to write "Ioannes" from the alphabet of Aries; I do not double 18, which is n, but write thus: 14, 16, 7, 18, 10, 23; or "abbas": 6, 7, 6, 23. With "Ioannes" [and] "abbas" one must act with like caution; for unless the operator be endowed with diligence, and know how to find greater things from small ones, he will not be a fit one to whom these least things of ours ought to be opened. Not everywhere are all things to be communicated to all, especially [those] whose use is convertible to good and ill. Moved reasonably by this consideration, we have plainly handed down very much in these six books of Polygraphy to those willing to know, but we have allowed far more secrets to lie hidden beneath what is manifest. Finally we have written a Key unfolding the whole work, so that in each [part] matter for exercising the memory may not be lacking, [while] from the reprobate—who are not willing to use them well—the cause of knowing these things may be taken away. Many mysteries lie hidden in single passages: the greater [things] you find from these, the more ample remain to be found. A way is prepared for beginners, in which, for those who advance, it will not be difficult, in the course of time, to find many rare and very great things. Here he who knew not will learn to write in Latin, [and] prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in a foreign tongue. But that he may understand not only his own mysteries which the unlearned man wraps up, but also the open speech of which he was hitherto always ignorant, it is a matter of no great labor, if the paraphrast shall have fully attained our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our Steganography, buried by reason, lest they lie open to unworthy babblers. Finally it was worth the labor that the work should not [pre]judge another, but that to each one his own right should be distributed inviolate. Wearied after a long voyage, here in this sea we fix our anchor under the name of Jesus Christ, Savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord's nativity one thousand five hundred and eight, in the eleventh Roman indiction, at Peapolis, city of the eastern Franks, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis. THE END.

[Decorative tailpiece.]

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, etc., On the Seven Secundeans—that is, Intelligences, or Spirits moving the spheres after God—a Booklet, embracing in itself many secrets worthy to be known, with wonderful brevity; dedicated to the Emperor, the Divine Maximilian, Augustus, Pious and Wise; composed from the archetype in the year 1545, and now again published. In the year of Christ 1600.

The booklet of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, on the celestial intelligences governing the spheres after God.

It is the opinion of very many of the ancients, most wise Caesar, that this lower world is governed, by the ordering of the first intellect, which is God, through secondary intelligences. Agreeing with their opinion, the Conciliator of the Physicians says that seven spirits were set over the seven planets from the beginning of heaven and earth. Each of these governs the world for three hundred and fifty-four years and four months in order. I make this position known to Your Most Sacred Majesty, not by affirming it, but only by reporting it.

[unclear]

The first angel, or spirit of Saturn, is called Orifiel; to him God entrusted the world to be governed from the beginning of creation, and his rule began on the fifteenth day of the month of March, in the first year of the world, and lasted 354 years and four months. Orifiel, however, is the name of an office, not of a nature, attributed to the spirit by reason of his action. Under his rule men were rude and rustic, dwelling in solitude after the manner of beasts. This needs no proof from me, since it is made plain to all from the text of Genesis.

The second governor of the world is Anael, spirit of Venus, who after Orifiel began to rule the influence of his planet in the year of the world 354, in the fourth month, that is, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of June; and he governed the world for 354 years and four months, down to the year 780 of the created globe, as is clear to one who calculates the age. Under the rule of this Anael men began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities, to discover manual arts, weaving, [laxificium], and things like these; also to indulge more abundantly in the pleasures of the flesh, to take beautiful wives for themselves, to forget God, and in many things to depart from natural simplicity, to invent games and songs, to play the cithara, and to devise whatever belongs to the principle and cultivation of Venus. This wantonness of life endured among men until the flood, taking the occasion of its own depravity.

On the Secondary [Intelligences]

The third, Zachariel, angel of Jupiter, began to govern the world in the year 780 from the creation of heaven and earth, in the eighth month, that is, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of October; and he governed the world for 354 years and four months, down to the year 1063 of the created globe inclusive. Under his governance men first began to claim lordship for themselves over one another, to practice hunting, to make [sentoria], and to adorn their bodies with various garments; and a great division arose between the good and the wicked, the good calling upon God, like Enoch, whom the Lord translated, while the wicked ran after the enticements of the flesh. Under the rule of this Zachariel men also began to live more civilly, to endure the laws of their elders, and to grow tame from their former savagery. Under his leadership, too, Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of necessary death. Finally, various inventions and arts of men emerged at this time, as the historians have set forth more clearly.

The fourth ruler of the world was Raphael, spirit of Mercury, who began in the year 1063 from the creation of heaven and earth, on the twenty-fourth day of February, and presided for 354 years and four months; and his dominion lasted down to the year of the world 1417 and the fourth month. In these times writing was first invented, and letters were first devised after the manner or form of trees and plants; these, however, later with time took on a more cultivated ornament and the appearance of characters, to their own

Little Book.

... the nations changed their own judgment. The use of musical instruments also began to multiply under the rule of this Raphael, and the first exchange of merchandise was invented among human beings. The rough daring of navigation, too, was first ventured in these times, and many other things of that sort.

[unclear]

The fifth governor of the world was Samael, the angel of Mars, who began on the 26th day of the month of June, in the year of the world 1417, and governed the world for 354 years and 4 months, until the year 1771, as is clearly evident from the history of Genesis. And it should be noted that the ancient philosophers handed down that whenever Samael, the spirit of Mars, is ruler of the globe, so often a notable alteration of monarchy arises. Religions and sects vary, laws and principalities are changed, and kingdoms are transferred to foreigners, as we can easily discover in order from histories. But Samael does not immediately from the beginning of his rule manifest this [unclear]; the same is to be understood concerning the spirits of the other planets, as is evident in histories, all of whom, according to the properties of the nature of their stars, influence and act upon the lower things of this world.

[unclear]

The sixth governor of the world was Gabriel of the Moon, who began after Samael of Mars on the 28th day of the month of October, in the year of the world 1771, in the eighth month, and governed the globe for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 2126.

On the Secondary Intelligences

In these times human beings were again multiplied and founded various cities. And it should be noted that the Hebrews say the flood occurred in the year of the world 1656, under the rule of Mars. But the Seventy interpreters, Isidore, and Bede confirm that it occurred in the year 2242, under the governance of Gabriel, spirit of the Moon; and this seems to me more consonant with the truth, by reason of the multiplication, which it is not the present time to explain.

The seventh governor of the world was Michael, angel of the Sun, who began on the 24th of February, in the year of the world, according to the common computation, 2126, and governed the globe for 354 years and four months, until the year of the world's age 2480 and 4 months. Under the rule of the angel of the Sun, as histories agree with the truth, kings first began to exist among mortals; among them Nimrod was the first, through lust for dominion, to seize tyrannical rule over his companions. The worship of gods was also instituted by human folly, and lesser men began to adore their princes as gods. Various arts too were invented by human beings at this time, namely mathematics, astronomy, magic; and the worship of the one God began to be offered to diverse creatures, and knowledge of the true God gradually passed into oblivion through human superstition. In these times, too, architecture was invented, and human beings began to use more refined customs and institutions.

The Origin of Kings.

The Source of Idolatry.

Next, in the eighth order, Orifiel, angel of Saturn, again began to govern the world on the 26th day of the month of June, in the year from the origin of the world 2480 and four months; and for 354 years and four months he governed the globe a second time, until the year of the world 2834 and the eighth month. Under the governance of this angel, peoples were multiplied, the earth was divided into regions, many kingdoms were established, the Tower of Babel was constructed, the confusion of tongues occurred, human beings were scattered over all the earth, and human beings began to cultivate the earth more carefully, to institute fields, sow grains, plant vineyards, set trees in the ground, and acquire with diligence whatever pertains to food and clothing. From this time the distinction of nobility first began to be made among human beings, when men who excelled the rest both in character and in ability received marks of glory from the greater men of the earth according to their merits. From this point the whole globe first began to come into human knowledge, since, as peoples were multiplied everywhere, many kingdoms also arose, and various differences of languages followed.

In the ninth order, Anael, spirit of Venus, again began to govern the world on the 29th day of October, in the year of the creation of heaven and earth 2834, in the eighth month, and presided for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 3189. In these times human beings, consigning the true God to oblivion, began to worship and honor the dead and their statues as God; this error occupied the world for more than two thousand years, introducing the increase of idolatry.

On the Secondary Intelligences

[unclear] curious adornments of the body and various kinds of musical instruments, men again pursued lust and the pleasure of the flesh excessively, and in these times men also set up and dedicated statues and temples to their gods. Incantations and sorceries were devised in those times by Zoroaster, first king of the Bactrians, though others say differently, whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, defeated in war.

In the tenth order Zachariel, the angel of Jupiter, again began to govern on the last day of the month of February, in the year from the creation of heaven and earth 3189, and governed, as usual, for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world itself 3543 and the fourth month. These were joyful times, which could truly be called golden, in which he brought abundance of all things and increase to the human race, and gave the world its greatest adornment. Likewise at this time God gave Abraham the law of circumcision, and first promised the redemption of the human race. Under his rule the patriarchs, founders of justice, shone forth in spirit, and the righteous were separated from the impious by their own will and deed. In these times also Jupiter was illustrious among the Arcadians, whom [Lisania?] calls the son of Heaven and of God, a king who first gave laws to the Arcadians, made them very civil in their customs, taught the worship of God, built temples, instituted priests, and procured many useful things for the human race; because of these things he was called Jupiter by them, and after death was held to be a god. Moreover, he took his origin from the sons of Heber, namely [Jerari?], as the histories report. Prometheus also, son of Atlas, under the rule of this angel was said to have made men, because from rude men he made them learned, humane, gentle, and polished in morals and knowledge; by art he made images move by themselves. He first devised the use of the ring, and likewise invented the sceptre, the diadem, and royal insignia. Other Jovian men also flourished in these times, very wise men and women, who by their own genius handed down many inventions useful to the human race; and because of the greatness of their wisdom, after death they were thought to have been numbered among the gods: namely Phoroneus, who first established laws and judgments among the Greeks, Sol, Minerva, Ceres, Serapis among the Egyptians, and many others.

In the eleventh order Raphael, the spirit of Mercury, again undertook the governance of the world on the first day of the month of July, in the year of the world 3543 and the fourth month, and presided for 354 years and 4 months, until the year from the creation of heaven and earth 3897 and the eighth month. In these times, as is clearly evident from the histories of the ancients, men devoted themselves more to wisdom; among them were these most illustrious men: Mercury, Bacchus, Omogyrus, Isis, Inachus, Argus, Apollo, Cecrops, and many others, who by their inventions benefited both the world of that time and the later world. Various superstitions too in the cultivation of idols were established by men in these times, and incantations and the arts of diabolical images were increased in a wondrous manner; and whatever subtlety and genius is usually attributed to Mercury was then being increased. Moses, a very wise leader of the Hebrews, skilled in many matters and arts, a worshipper of the true and one God, vindicated the Hebrew people from the slavery of the Egyptians into freedom. Around this time Saturn, who taught that fields should be fertilized with dung, was held as a god. Cadmus, inventor of letters, first reigned in Italy; after him Saturn, who was powerful under the rule of this Raphael, angel of Mercury. He gave the law to his people through Moses in writing, which bears manifest witness to the future birth of Christ in the flesh. A wondrous diversity of religions also arose in the world. Many Sibyls too flourished in these times, prophets, soothsayers, haruspices, magi, seers, such as the Erythraean Sibyl, the Delphic, the Phrygian, and the others.

In the twelfth order, Samael, the angel of Mars, began again to rule the world on the second day of the month of October, in the year of the world 3892, in the eighth month; and his rule lasted 354 years and 4 months, down to the year 4252. Under his rule occurred that great and most famous destruction of Troy in Asia Minor, and there took place a remarkable change of monarchy and of many kingdoms, and the founding anew of many cities, such as Paris, Mainz, Carthage, Naples, and many others.

The destruction of Troy. [unclear]

Paris. [unclear]

Mainz. [unclear]

Booklet.

Many kingdoms also arose anew, such as those of the Lacedaemonians, the Corinthians, the Hebrews, and very many others. In these times there were very great wars and battles of kings and peoples throughout the whole world, and various changes of empires. From this time the Venetians reckon the beginning both of their people and of their city from the Trojans. And it should be noted that very many other nations, both in Europe and in Asia, claim that they took their origin from the Trojans; I have judged that only so much credence should be granted them as they themselves will be able to persuade me, by sufficient testimony, belongs to the truth. Frivolous are the things they adduce about their nobility and antiquity, wishing openly to boast, as though there had not been peoples in Europe before the destruction of the Trojans, and as though no one among them were ignoble.

Likewise, under the rule of this planet Saul was made the first king of the Jews, and afterward David, whose son King Solomon built in Jerusalem the temple of the true God, most famous in all the world. From this time the Spirit of God, illuminating his prophets with a fuller light of his grace, caused them to foretell not only the future incarnation of the Lord Savior, but many other things as well, as the sacred histories testify. Among them were Nathan, prophet of King David, Gad, Asaph, Ahijah, Shemaiah, Azariah, Anan, with many others. Homer, the Greek poet and writer of the destruction of Troy, Dares the Phrygian, and Dictys of Crete, who were present at that destruction and likewise described it, are read to have been alive in these times.

Origin of the Venetians.

Saul.

Homer.

On the Secondary Intelligences

[unclear]

In the thirteenth order, Gabriel, the spirit of the Moon, again took up the rule of the world on the thirtieth day of January, in the year from the origin of the universe 4252, and he presided in his empire for 354 years and 4 months, down to the year of the world 4606 and the fourth month. In that time many prophets flourished among the Hebrews, namely Elijah, Elisha, Micah, Obadiah, and very many others. And there were various changes in the kingdom of the Hebrews. Lycurgus gave rights and laws to the Lacedaemonians. Capetus Silvius, Lyberius Silvius, Romulus Silvius, and Numitor, kings of Italy, flourished under this spirit. Many new kingdoms also took their beginnings under him, such as those of the Lydians, the Medes, the Spartans, and others. The monarchy of the Assyrians failed with Sardanapalus. Likewise the kingdom of the Macedonians came to an end. Various laws were imposed upon men, and the worship of the true God was neglected; the religion of false gods was propagated exceedingly. The city of Rome was built under the rule of this spirit in the year 1484, which was the 239th year of the rule of Gabriel himself in this order; and the kingdom of the Silvii of Italy failed, and that of the Romans began. In these times also Thales, Solon, Periander, Cleobulus, Bias, and Pittacus, the seven sages, flourished in Greece, and from then on philosophers and poets began to be held in esteem. The first to rule at Rome was Romulus, founder of the city, for 37 years, a fratricide and cultivator of sedition. After him Numa Pompilius ruled for 42 years; he enlarged the worship of the gods, in the time of Hezekiah, king of the Jews

Little Book.

12

[unclear] kept the kingdom in great peace. Near the end of the government of this spirit of the Moon, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took Jerusalem and destroyed King Zedekiah, and led all the people away captive. Jeremiah the prophet flourished, who foretold this destruction, and likewise the future liberation from Babylon.

Nebuchadnezzar. Zedekiah. Jeremiah.

After Gabriel, Michael, spirit of the Sun, again assumed the fourteenth rule of the world; it began on the first day of the month of May, in the year of the world 4606, in the fourth month, and he ruled the world in his order for 354 years, until the year 4960 from the creation of the world, and 8 months. In the time of this governance Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon, restored liberty and a king to the people of the Hebrews, under the direction of Michael, who, Daniel writes, stood for the people of the Jews, to whom they had been committed by God. Likewise in these times the monarchy of the kingdom of the Persians began; its first king was Darius, and the second Cyrus, who utterly destroyed that most powerful kingdom of Babylon in the days of Belshazzar, as Daniel and the prophets had foretold. In these times the Cumaean Sibyl flourished; she offered nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus to be bought for a price, in which was contained the sequence of future warnings and the rationale of the whole commonwealth of the Romans. But when the king refused the price, the Sibyl burned the first three books in his sight; for the remaining six she asked the same price. When he again refused it, she also handed three others over to the fire to be burned,

On the Secondary Intelligences

which she would have done with the last ones as well, had not the king, persuaded by the counsel of his men, redeemed them from destruction by paying the price that had been demanded for all. Likewise, after abolishing kings, the Romans established two consuls for each year. Phalaris the tyrant occupied Sicily in those times. Magic too at those times was held in great esteem among the kings of the Persians. Pythagoras the philosopher and many others among the Greeks then flourished. The temple and city at Jerusalem were rebuilt. Ezra the prophet restored from memory, using it as his archetype, the books of Moses burned by the Chaldeans, who were also called Babylonians. Xerxes, king of the Persians, led an army against the Greeks, but accomplished little. Rome was taken, burned, and destroyed by the Gauls, except only the Capitol, guarded by a goose, which roused the weary fighters. The very famous wars of the Athenians also took place in those times. Socrates and Plato the philosophers lived at that time. The Romans, again abolishing the consuls, established tribunes and aediles, and in these times were involved in many calamities. Alexander the Great also, after the governance of Michael had been completed, reigned in Macedonia. He destroyed the monarchy of the Persians in Darius, and subjected all Asia, with part of Europe, to his rule. He lived 125 years and five months; after his death endless wars and many evils followed, and the monarchy was divided into four. Among the Hebrews contention began over the high priesthood. The kingdom of Syria began. After-

Booklet.

After Michael, fifteenth in order, now for the third time Orifiel, the spirit of Saturn, took up the government of the world on the last day of the month of September, in the year of the creation of the universe 4960, month 8, and he presided for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 5315. Under his government the Punic War began between the Romans and the Carthaginians. The Punic War. The city of Rome was almost utterly consumed by fire and water. The calamity of Rome. The Colossus, a cast bronze image 126 feet high, fell in an earthquake. The Colossus is destroyed. In this one year there was peace for the Romans after the Punic War; for 440 years they had never been without war. Jerusalem, together with the temple, was burned and destroyed by Antiochus Epiphanes. Antiochus Epiphanes. The history and wars of the Maccabees took place. In these times, in the year 606 from the founding of the city, Carthage was destroyed and burned for 17 continuous days. Carthage is destroyed. In Sicily there was a conspiracy of 70,000 slaves against their masters. In those times great portents were seen in Europe: domestic animals fled to the woods; blood flowed; a fiery globe flashed from heaven with a crash. Many portents. Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, waged war with the Romans for 40 years. Mithridates. The kingdom of the Hebrews was restored, which had been interrupted for 575 years, from the time of Zedekiah until Aristobulus. Likewise the German Teutons invaded the Romans, and after many battles are said to have been defeated, and 160,000 slain, besides innumerable others who killed themselves along with their households, under the consuls Caius and Manlius. The Teutonic disaster against the Romans. Nevertheless many of the Romans had previously been destroyed by them. Finally the civil wars, which lasted 40 years, greatly wore down the Romans.

On the Secondary Intelligences

Three suns appeared at Rome; not for long, but soon they were reduced into one. A few years later Julius Caius Caesar usurped the empire of the Romans; after him Octavian Augustus enlarged it and united Asia, Africa, and Europe into one monarchy. He ruled for 36 years; through him God bestowed peace on the whole world. In the year from the founding of the city 751, in the 42nd year of Octavian Caesar Augustus, in the 245th year and 8th month of the prescribed government of Orifiel, the spirit of Saturn, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of December, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem of Judaea. Note how beautiful is the ordering of divine providence. For the world was first created under the government of Orifiel, and also under the third was mercifully redeemed, restored, and renewed, so that it may seem to furnish a harmony for this description of the sevenfold government of the world. For in the first government of Orifiel there was one monarchy of the whole; under the second, as we said above, it was divided into many. Again under the third, as is seen, it was recalled into unity; although, if we measure rightly, it also becomes manifest that in the second government of Orifiel there was one monarchy of the whole world, when the tower of Babylon was being built. From this point the kingdom of the Jews was taken away, and the victims and continual sacrifice ceased; nor will liberty be restored to the Jews before the third revolution

Booklet.

the [unclear] of the spirit Michael; and this will take place after the birth of Christ in the year 1880, month 8, that is, in the year of the world 7170, month 8. In those times many of the Jews and gentiles took up the Christian religion, while very simple and rustic men preached, whom not human instruction but the Spirit of God had illumined. Then the world began to be recalled to the first innocence of simplicity, while Orifiel, the spirit of Saturn, governed it throughout. Heavenly things were mixed with earthly; many Christians too, for the faith which they preached, were cruelly slain by the rulers of the world. Around the end of Orifiel's rule Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, and the Jews were scattered over all the earth, 1,100,000 being killed and 80,000 sold; the rest fled, and so the Romans utterly destroyed Judea.

[unclear]

Sixteenth in order, after Orifiel, Anael, the spirit of Venus, resumed the governance of the whole world for the third time on the last day of January, in the year from the creation of heaven and earth 5315, but from the birth of Christ 109, and he governed the world for 354 years and 4 months, up to the year of the world 5669, month 4, and of the Lord's Nativity [unclear] 463. And it should be noted that through almost the whole time of this rule of the Angel of Venus the Church of the Christians flourished and prevailed amid persecutions, with countless thousands of men slain for the faith of Christ. Finally, several heresies began to sprout in the Church in these times, which in due course were extinguished not without the labor and blood of good men.

On the Secondary Intelligences.

Many men shone in those times, most learned and most eloquent in every kind of knowledge: theologians, astronomers, physicians, orators, historiographers, and the like, not only among the gentiles but also among the Christians. At last the persecution of unbelievers against the Church ceased, after Constantine the Great Caesar took up the faith, in the year of the world 5539, after the midpoint of the rule of Anael himself, the Angel of Venus; although even afterwards it was at times disturbed in part by the impious, nevertheless on the whole it remained very quiet for a long time. From then on the human race, which from the time of King Ninus had miserably wandered for 2300 years in the worship of idols, was mercifully recalled to the knowledge of the one God. Various arts of subtlety were increased in these times, and through the correspondences of nature took on adornment and growth. For men's customs change with time, and lower bodies are disposed according to the influence of the higher. The mind indeed is free, and does not receive the influence of the stars unless, through the excessive commerce which it has with the body, by inclining itself it stains its own affection. For the angels who are the movers of the spheres destroy or overturn none of the things which nature has established. A comet of unusual magnitude preceded Constantine's death. The Arian heresy disturbed the holy Church in many places at the end of this rule. In the time of Julian Caesar crosses appeared on the linen garments of men.

Booklet.

In Asia and Palestine wars, plagues, and famines followed in those places in which the crosses had appeared. In these times also, around the year of the Lord 360, the Franks had their beginning in Germany; afterwards, when they had devastated Gaul, they called the conquered land Francia after their own name. The origin or beginnings of the German Franks. The description of Francia was great in length and breadth; its metropolis was Mainz, but now only Würzburg. Mainz, formerly the metropolis of the Franks. Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Saxons, Thuringians, and the surrounding bishoprics today occupy a great part of Francia in Germany. Likewise, in year 280 of this Anael's governance, the Roman Empire began to decline, when the city was captured and burned by the Goths, the imperial seat having previously been transferred under Constantine into Greece; this was the beginning and cause of the whole decline of the monarchy. The decline of the Roman Empire. For around the end of this rule of Anael there arose Radagistes and Athaulf, kings of the Goths; likewise afterwards Genseric of the Vandals, and Attila of the Huns, who miserably tore the empire apart, as is clear in these histories. Invasions of the Goths, Vandals, and Huns.

[unclear]

After Anael, seventeenth in order, Zachariel, the spirit of Jupiter, resumed the universal governance for the third time on the first day of June, in the year of the world 5669, month 4, but of the Lord's Nativity 463, month 7; and he presided for 354 years and four months, up to the year of the world 6023 and month 8, but of the Lord 817. Many in these times, out of love for Christian philosophy, betook themselves to the desert; many portents also appeared,

A comet, an earthquake, a rain of blood. Merlin. Arthur. Thirty kingdoms served Arthur. The orders of monks. Boethius. The disturbed condition of the Church and the empire. Clovis, good king of France.

A comet, an earthquake, a rain of blood. Merlin, born in [Tumba?], foretold wondrous things at the beginning of this rule. Arthur, whom in the common tongue they call Arthur, the most famous king of Britain, conquered the barbarians, restored peace to the Church, victoriously fought many battles, enlarged the faith of Christ, and subjected all Gaul, Norway, Denmark, and many provinces to his empire. He was the most glorious of all the kings of his time; after many splendid deeds had been accomplished, he appeared nowhere, though the Britons expected him to return for many years. Concerning him the mimes once produced marvelous songs. While he reigned, England was in flower, and thirty kingdoms served him. In these times the orders of monks began to multiply in the Church of God. Theodoric, Arian king of the Goths, possessed all Italy and killed the consul Boethius. Everything was full of disturbance, the empire and the Church alike. The emperors Zeno and Anastasius, Arians in the East, Theodoric and his successors in Italy, and Honorius, king of the Vandals, in Africa, were exercising no small tyranny. At last Clovis, king of the Franks in Gaul, having become a Christian, both overcame the Goths and imposed peace, though not everywhere on earth, in the time of Saint Benedict, in the five-hundredth year of the Christians, or thereabouts, at the beginning of this rule of the angel Zachariel of Jupiter, whose special property it is to change spirits, empires, and kingdoms; that this was done in this revolution the histories declare in many ways, and what the angel Raphael himself could not do

Little Book.

...was almost submerged by the waves of the sea, and more than 100,000 persons perished. The Tartars devastated Hungary and Poland, after first overcoming Greater Armenia and many regions.

The discovery of a book by a Jew. In the year of the Christians 1244, a certain Jew at Toledo, while digging, found a book in which it was written: “In the third world Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary, and will suffer for the salvation of men.” Soon believing, he was baptized. The third world was the third revolution of the spirit of Saturn, of which mention was made above; at its beginning Christ was born of the Virgin.

Frederick deprived of the empire. The Roman pontiffs, removing Frederick from the empire, said that it had been vacant for twenty-eight years [unclear] Wilhelm, count of Holland; Conrad, son of Frederick; Alfonso, king of Castile; and Richard, count of Cornwall, brother of the king of England; and evils were multiplied on the earth.

The confederation of the Swiss. At this time, around the year of the Lord 1260, the confederation of the Swiss first began: a people small in number, which grew with time. They killed many of the nobles, and drove others from their territories; warlike men, whose commonwealth is known to all the peoples of Germany.

Rudolf of Habsburg. Origin of the dukes of Austria. In the year of the Christians 1273, Rudolf of Habsburg was made emperor by the election of the princes, and he ruled for eighteen years: a man in every respect prudent and excellent, from whom all the later dukes of Austria descended. The Tartars...

On the Secundei

[unclear] the lands of the Christians, invading Constantinople and Greece, they inflicted great losses on the Christians. The Saracens occupy many cities in Asia, and kill more than four hundred thousand Christians.

When Rudolf had died, Adolf of Nassau was elected king and ruled for six years; afterward Albert, son of Rudolf, defeated him in battle near Worms, killed him, and was elected emperor in the year 1298. He ruled for ten years and was killed by his brother's son. The Order of the Templars is destroyed by order of Pope Clement V. The island of Rhodes was taken by Christians from the hands of the Saracens, in the fourth year of the siege and of continuous war against them. After Albert was killed by his nephew, Henry VIII, count of Luxembourg, was appointed emperor; he ruled for five years. When he had died, Louis IV of Bavaria ruled for thirty-two years, beginning in the year 1315; to him the Roman pontiffs gave the crown. Frederick, duke of Austria, opposed him, but was defeated by him.

After Louis, Charles IV, king of Bohemia, was appointed emperor; he raised the bishopric of Prague to an archbishopric, and ruled for thirty-one years. There were very great earthquakes. This Charles newly instituted many things concerning tolls in favor of the prince-electors. Gunther, count of Schwarzenburg, calling himself king, opposed Emperor Charles, but prevailed in nothing against him. After Charles, his son Wenceslaus ruled for twenty-two years; after him Jodocus, margrave of Moravia, succeeded Sigismund, brother of Wenceslaus.

Little Book

Wenceslaus was deposed. Leopold, duke of Austria, fighting in battle with eight counts and more than 4,000 men, was killed by the Swiss. Under Wenceslaus, king of the Bohemians and emperor, the doctrine of the Hussites took its beginning. When he had been deposed, Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, was elected and ruled for ten years. In the year of the Lord 1369 the Christians brought war upon the Saracens, but it turned out badly because of the arrogance of the French, since more than 100,000 of our men perished, besides captives, among whom was John, duke of the Burgundians. There were many wars in these times.

In the year 1407 Sigismund becomes emperor for twenty-seven years. He attempted to lay waste Bohemia for the extirpation of heresies, but made little progress. The kingdom of France is cruelly ravaged and afflicted by the English and Burgundians. When Sigismund had died, Albert, duke of Austria, his son-in-law, succeeded him in the year of the Christians 1438, and ruled for only two years, a very excellent man and worthy of empire. When he had died, Frederick III, duke of Austria, [son?], was appointed emperor by election of the princes, and ruled for fifty-six years, a man divine in intellect and peaceful in spirit. He began to reign in the year of the Lord 1440.

In the year of the Christians 1453 Constantinople is taken by the Turks through the betrayal of a certain Genoese, and gradually all Greece fell away from the Christian faith. Moreover, in this time many kingdoms and provinces of the Christians are ravaged and seized by the Turks. The Christians [unclear] much wars

Mainz is captured.
